title: A developer’s path through a small STARK program
description: Trace, constraints, commitments, a small teaching ISA, program pinning, and four traps. A bounded walkthrough without unmeasured proof claims.
origin: Bounded adaptation of preview-article.html and supplied Grok tutorial note
body:
Scope of this walkthrough

This note is adapted from a tutorial draft without a reproducible benchmark record. Code blocks are sketches, not a complete crate compiled by this site.

rust-stark-zkvm is a small STARK machine: arithmetic, forward branches, a fixed register file, Winterfell proving, and HTTP/MCP interfaces. The documented verifier re-executes public programs. Private witnesses, a general memory argument, and recursion are outside that documented scope. Do not read this page as a second, larger machine.

Trace, constraints, commitment

A STARK-shaped system still answers three questions. What happened is an execution trace: one row per cycle, one column per piece of state. Was it legal is a set of constraints, polynomials that are zero on an honest trace. Can a verifier check without reading the whole table is a commitment, usually a Merkle root reduced by FRI.

Hold that triad. Later terms such as query count or grinding are adjustments to the commitment and the soundness error. They are not a reason to skip naming the program, the inputs, and the claimed output.

A small teaching ISA

A teaching ISA can stay small on purpose. Each instruction widens the trace or raises constraint degree. The draft used eight operations — add, sub, mul, conditional jumps, load, store, and halt — over 16 registers with R0 hardwired to zero. That is a teaching shape. It is not the instruction list proven by the current rust-stark-zkvm card.

pub enum Op { Add, Sub, Mul, Jz, Jnz, Load, Store, Halt }

// Sketch only. Not a crate that this site compiled.
// A verifier should pin the program image, not "some program".

The useful security decision in that sketch is the program identity. A proof is about a specific program. If the verifier only checks that some AIR of the right shape accepted a proof, a different program can be substituted. Pin the program hash at the application boundary. The published zkVM card still says to read the AIR and the proof object in the repository before assuming that pin exists.

Execution and determinism

An executor is a fold: fetch, decode, write the next row. Determinism is the requirement. The prover and any re-execution must agree bit for bit, so wall clocks and hash-map iteration order do not belong in the semantics. The draft’s executor used a HashMap for memory. That is a bad place for iteration order to leak into a trace. If you build memory, give it an explicit order.

An AIR constraint for addition, written as a sentence, is: on an add cycle, the next destination register equals the current destination plus the source; on other cycles the add flag is zero and that constraint is idle. Boundary constraints can pin the first program counter and the final halt flag. Degree matters because higher-degree constraints cost more in the proof, but flattening a constraint with a helper column can also make it unsound. Write the obvious constraint first. This note has no timing table for that tradeoff.

Constraint boundaries

// Sketch of one transition, not Winterfell’s real API.
f_add * (next(rd) - rd - rs)

Winterfell is the library rust-stark-zkvm lists. Calling a two-line prove() in a blog post is not evidence that this site ran it, and it is not the library’s actual function signature. Read the crate in the repository.

Benchmark traps

The tutorial draft supplied benchmark figures without a source revision, exact parameters, or a measurement record. Those figures are not published here.

Three traps are still worth keeping, without the fake table. Nondeterminism: a timestamp or an unordered map in the semantics makes the prover and the verifier disagree. Padding: traces are often padded to a power of two, so a short program still pays for the next power. Benchmark theater: a proof size without hardware, field, security bits, and thread count is an advertisement. A fourth trap is trace bloat: unnecessary columns increase the data processed by the prover.

Security parameters

“96-bit security” is not a mood. It is a claim about the field, the number of FRI queries, and any grinding bits, taken together. A proof envelope that does not carry those parameters cannot be compared with another envelope. This page does not assert a security level for rust-stark-zkvm.

Negative control, matching the repository’s own review note: change the claimed result or the program and confirm rejection. A single accepted proof does not show that the verifier rejects anything else. Recursion cost below 2^16 rows, memory channels, and CI proof gates are not established by this note.

Next reading

Next reading on this site: the STARK explanation, the one-page verifiable-computation note, and the rust-stark-zkvm project card. The source of truth is the repository, not this tutorial draft.

title: What Are STARK Proofs? A Plain-English Technical Overview
description: What STARK proofs are, how traces, constraints and commitments interact, and why they need no trusted setup — a plain-English technical overview with code diagrams.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The three questions every proof answers

What happened? An execution trace: one row per cycle, columns for registers, flags, and memory channels -- the computation flattened into a table. Was it legal? Constraints: polynomials over current and next row that vanish on every honest trace; a single violated row makes the polynomial nonzero and the proof impossible to produce. Can I check cheaply? Commitments: the trace is hashed into Merkle trees, then the FRI protocol reduces checking "these millions of rows satisfy these polynomials" to verifying a few dozen authenticated samples. Hold that triad -- trace, constraints, commitment -- and every exotic term in the literature becomes an optimization of one of its legs.

Why there is no trusted setup

Anatomy of a real proof blob

  • Trace commitments: Merkle roots for the main and auxiliary (memory/permutation) trace segments.
  • Constraint composition + FRI layers: folded polynomials, each layer committed, ending in a constant.
  • Query openings: ~30-60 sets of Merkle paths proving sampled positions match the commitments.
  • Grinding nonce: proof-of-work bits binding the prover to the challenge transcript.
  • Public values: outputs and pinned identities (the vkey hash) the verifier checks in the clear.

Size follows directly from that list: more queries and bigger fields grow the blob; longer computations barely do, because FRI folds logarithmically. That asymmetry -- proof size logarithmic in runtime -- is the entire commercial argument, and the companion Q&A on why STARK proofs are larger than SNARKs explains the constant factors honestly.

What verification actually costs

Verifying means: recompute challenges from the transcript, evaluate the composed constraint at sampled points, walk Merkle paths. On a laptop this is single-digit milliseconds and a few megabytes of RAM; on a microcontroller, tiny-verify does it in 4 KB of C. Compare the prover's seconds and you see the STARK bargain: expensive once, cheap forever, for everyone, without secrets -- which is precisely the shape you want when the verifier is a browser, a contract, or a regulator's script.

Where STARKs earn their keep today

Proof-carrying CI (benchmarks and supply-chain metadata attested per commit), verifiable batch jobs whose consumers will never rerun them, privacy-preserving compliance predicates (prove the dataset satisfies the rule, not the dataset), and educational tooling where transparency is the point. The developer tutorial in this cluster builds each layer hands-on; the STARK vs SNARK comparison helps you choose; and the cluster index maps the rest, from execution traces to FRI deep dives in production next batches.

Three misconceptions to unlearn

That last reframe decides most real deployments: the nightly proving job costs less than one engineer's coffee break, and buys every downstream consumer the ability to re-verify for free, forever, without asking anyone's permission. The economics of proof systems are batch economics, and reading them as interactive economics is why some pilots die concluded "too slow" when the truth was "wrong shape". Every remaining article in this cluster assumes the batch reading, and says so explicitly whenever an interactive exception earns its place.

Do STARKs reveal anything about the inputs?

The proof commits to the trace without opening it except at sampled positions, which are masked by random blinding polynomials in honest implementations. Public outputs and the pinned program identity are visible by design; everything else stays hidden. Zero-knowledge is a property you must preserve in parameter choices, not one you get for free from the acronym.

title: STARK vs SNARK: Which Proof System Should You Ship?
description: STARK vs SNARK compared on proof size, prover time, trusted setup, post-quantum safety and ecosystem maturity, with a decision table for choosing what to ship.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The decision table

Measure this comparison on your own workload. No timing or memory table from the draft is presented as an observed result.

Read the table by column of consequence, not by row: if your verifier is a smart contract paying gas per byte, proof size dominates and SNARKs win despite setup pain. If your verifier is a server, browser, or CI job, verification milliseconds are free and STARK transparency plus prover speed dominate. The middle column -- modern universal-setup SNARKs -- is where recursion ecosystems live, and where most "STARK vs SNARK" debates actually resolve into "which recursion stack".

Proof size versus prover time, honestly

Trust models: ceremonies versus hash functions

A Groth16 setup concentrates existential risk: whoever holds the toxic waste can forge proofs forever, so communities run multiparty ceremonies with public audits -- admirable, complex, and forever tied to the ceremony's integrity story. STARKs replace that story with "SHA-2 is preimage-resistant", a claim auditors can test and decades-old hardware can verify. For sovereignty-focused infrastructure -- archives, federations, compliance artifacts meant to outlive their builders -- setup-free soundness is not a technical preference but an archival property: a proof whose trust depends on a 2019 ceremony video is a proof with a expiry date nobody signed.

The quantum footnote, sized correctly

Choosing in one paragraph

On-chain verification or byte-budgeted verifiers: SNARK, preferring universal-setup families unless gas per byte forces Groth16. Off-chain verification, long computations, transparency requirements, or archival lifetimes: STARK, as implemented in the zkVM tutorial and rust-stark-zkvm. Recursion-heavy roadmaps: evaluate both, because aggregation changes the economics -- the cluster's recursion Q&A (in production next) documents where STARK-of-STARKs currently breaks even. And when a vendor answers "which proof system?" with a brand name before asking your verifier environment and artifact lifetime, you have learned something useful about the vendor.

Hybrid patterns: composition as insurance

The operational lesson is mundane but decisive: manage the envelopes as one lifecycle. A wrapper whose inner proof rotated unnoticed is a lie with valid syntax, so pinning, manifests, and rotation schedules must span the composition, not its parts. A third pattern is temporal: launch with the system your verifier demands today while archiving the artifacts tomorrow's migration needs -- traces or re-provable inputs, parameter documentation, hashes of everything. Proof-system portability is not a technical feature, it is a record-keeping discipline. Teams that treat proof-system choice as a marriage discover divorce costs; teams that treat it as a dated, documented decision migrate twice without incident. The table above chooses your starting system; this section chooses your exits -- and in sovereignty engineering, the exits are half the design.

Can I convert proofs between systems later?

Partially: wrapping a STARK inside a SNARK (for cheap on-chain checks) is a standard composition, and the reverse direction adds nothing useful. Composition inherits the outer system's trust model for the wrapped claim, so archival artifacts should keep the inner STARK verifiable standalone -- store both, verify the one your era trusts.

Do STARKs ever beat SNARKs on proof size?

At very high security levels with recursive aggregation, STARK stacks can approach kilobyte-scale amortized proofs while SNARKs grow setup or verifier complexity -- but for single small proofs, no: SNARKs own the byte budget. Size comparisons without trace length and security bits are marketing in both directions.

Which has better tooling for beginners?

title: How to Build a zkVM in Rust: ISA to Proof in Nine Steps
description: How to build a zero-knowledge VM in Rust in nine steps: ISA design, trace emission, AIR constraints, Winterfell proving, verification keys and a proving API.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Steps 1-3: ISA, executor, trace

Start from the ZKVM-ISA v1 shape: eight instructions, sixteen registers, R0 zero. Resist adding opcodes early -- every instruction is a permanent column-and-constraint tax, and growth should cost an argument. The executor is a pure function (program, inputs) -> Vec<Row>: no clocks, no hashmap iteration in semantics, wrapping arithmetic explicit, cycle budget asserted. Determinism is not hygiene here, it is the security model: prover and verifier-side re-executions must agree bit-for-bit or proofs become lottery tickets. Emit the trace with padding visible (power-of-two length, idle rows with sleeping flags) so cost is honest from day one -- the padding economics and boundary-crossing alerts are detailed in the trace article.

Steps 4-6: AIR, backend, pinning

Write constraints as flag-times-relation (degree 2), boundary assertions pinning pc, inputs, and halt, and one auxiliary pair for the memory permutation argument -- the minimal receipt set from the AIR article. Hand the trace and AIR to Winterfell per the prover tutorial: proving and verification arrive as library calls, and your remaining job is the pinning layer the library explicitly does not do -- assert the program-image hash at verification, log it, alert on mismatch. Steps five and six are where most hobby zkVMs stop being toys: without pinning, your verifier accepts arithmetic rather than claims, a distinction the verification-failure Q&A ranks as cause number one in production incidents.

Steps 7-9: API, gates, benchmarks

Wrap prove/verify in an HTTP or MCP surface with idempotent, content-addressed jobs (retries free, caches honest), then wire two CI gates: a proof round-trip gate proving and verifying a canonical program per commit, and a drift matrix gate running the four mutation classes from the verification Q&A so parameter drift fails merges instead of deployments. Finally, publish benchmarks with the full manifest -- hardware, field, security bits, threads, trace lengths -- and regression-alert on proof-time and proof-size slopes, because silent slope changes are how provers rot. The rust-stark-zkvm repository is this nine-step machine grown up: same skeleton, plus recursion experiments, MCP tools, and a benchmark dashboard whose negative results are cited more than its positive ones.

The three decisions that age with you

  • Memory model early. Append-only log with permutation consistency costs columns but streams; RAM-style models cost less width and more prover memory. Choose once, document forever.
  • Field and security as configuration, never code. Manifest-carried parameters with verifier assertions keep upgrades deployable instead of archaeological.
  • Spec before features. Write the ISA document when the ISA is eight instructions; updating a spec is cheap, reconstructing one from a grown codebase is not -- a lesson every maintained proof system's changelog eventually confesses.

Ship the nine steps in a weekend; spend the following month on the three decisions, because the weekend code is replaceable and the decisions are the system. Contributors arrive for the proof magic and stay for the clarity of a machine whose every column can name the constraint that binds it -- the column census from the AIR article is the interview they pass on arrival.

One warning earned from reviewing first zkVMs: resist the temptation to optimize the prover before the pinning layer exists. A fast prover with loose verification is a fast liar, and the pinning plus drift-gate steps are twenty lines that convert speed into something worth measuring. Build the nine steps in order, let the gates fail your own commits for a week, and only then open the benchmark dashboard -- by which point its slopes and ceilings will mean something, because everything upstream of them will finally be true.

And when a contributor's first pull request lands -- usually a mutation test for a constraint they broke during onboarding -- welcome them the way the mentorship program does: with the design notes, the benchmark dashboard, and the standing invitation to break things in a branch until the machines explain why. Proof systems grow the way all infrastructure grows: one reviewed decision at a time, written down where the next person can find it.

How small can the ISA stay and still be useful?
Should recursion be in v1?
What is the hardest step for first-time builders?

Consistently: the memory permutation argument. Registers feel natural, flags feel mechanical, but "reads return the last write" as a local constraint requires the auxiliary-column trick to click. Budget a focused evening for it with the tutorial's aux section open; after it clicks, everything else is assembly of understood parts, and the click is the moment builders report finally understanding what proofs bind.

title: Winterfell Prover Tutorial: A Small STARK Design Walkthrough
description: A Winterfell prover tutorial: define a trace, register AIR constraints, produce your first STARK proof and verify it — with illustrative Rust snippets.

Setup and the mental split

Everything you write lives in two traits. The Trace trait fills a matrix of base-field elements row by row from your execution -- deterministic, no randomness, no clocks. The Air trait declares degrees, boundary constraints (first/last row pins), and transition constraints over a frame of current and next rows. Winterfell infers the rest: composition polynomial, DEEP queries, proof serialization format. Respecting that split is the whole tutorial; fighting it (randomness in traces, I/O in constraints) is the whole failure mode.

title: AIR Constraints Explained: Binding Execution Traces with Polynomials
description: AIR constraints explained: how polynomial transition and boundary constraints bind execution traces, plus degree costs and the flattening tricks that keep proofs small.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The vanishing principle, concretely

Transition constraints: one sentence per instruction

Boundary constraints: pinning the story's ends

Transition constraints prove local legality; boundary constraints anchor global meaning: first-row pc equals zero, input registers carry the public inputs, last row has halt set and outputs in agreed columns. Without them, a perfectly legal trace of a different computation would verify -- constraints bind shape, boundaries bind identity. Keep the boundary set minimal and public: every pinned value becomes part of the public inputs the verifier checks in the clear, and bloated public inputs bloat the proof envelope and leak witness structure you may not want visible. The pinning instinct connects directly to vkey pinning at the application layer, the pair of checks the verification-failure Q&A ranks as causes one and two.

Auxiliary columns: receipts for running claims

Testing constraints: negative tests are the specification

How do I keep constraint degree low when semantics feel multiplicative?

Introduce an auxiliary or flag column that carries the product once, then reference it linearly everywhere else -- pay width in base or extension field instead of degree in the composition polynomial. If the multiplication is between two dynamic values you both need elsewhere, name the product as its own column with its own defining constraint; degrees stay at 2 and the column doubles as a debuggable intermediate in trace dumps.

Can constraints reference rows beyond t+1?
What makes an AIR unsound in practice?

Under-constrained columns: a register nobody binds on non-flag rows can drift freely between uses, and drift that never affects outputs is invisible to tests yet exploitable by a malicious prover crafting alternative witnesses. The audit is simple and brutal: for every column, name the constraint that binds every row; columns that only bind conditionally need a default relation (value carries) or removal. This column census catches more real unsoundness than any amount of positive testing.

title: The FRI Protocol Explained Simply: Commitments, Folds, Queries
description: The FRI protocol explained simply: polynomial commitment, folding rounds, query sampling and soundness — what each step proves and what it costs the prover.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The job FRI does in one paragraph

Constraints reduce correctness to "this committed table is a low-degree polynomial evaluated on a domain". Commitments (Merkle roots) let the verifier request authenticated values, but Merkle alone cannot answer the global question "is the underlying function low-degree?" -- a table of random noise commits just fine. FRI answers exactly that question probabilistically: it does not read the polynomial, it interrogates its structure through folds and samples. The soundness statement is proximity: if the committed function is far from any polynomial of the claimed degree, FRI rejects except with negligible probability; if it is close, the decoded polynomial is unique, and the constraints evaluated on it carry the computational claim. Everything else in a STARK is bookkeeping around this interrogation.

Folding: halving with a challenge

Write the polynomial in even/odd parts, f(x) = e(x²) + x·o(x²). Given a verifier challenge α, define the folded function f₁(y) = e(y) + α·o(y): degree halves, and knowing f₁ plus the commitment to f ties the two together at paired points ±x. Repeat log-times until a constant remains. Each layer is committed before the next challenge is derived (Fiat-Shamir from the transcript), so the prover cannot adapt layers to future folds. The verifier's work per query is a pairwise consistency check down the layer stack: open f at ±x, open f₁ at x², check the folding relation with α -- log-depth arithmetic over Merkle paths, which is why verification stays millisecond-fast even for million-row traces, as the measurements in the STARK overview show.

Queries, grinding, and where the bytes go

DEEP queries: sampling where it matters

Plain FRI samples the committed trace at random domain points, but constraint checks happen at composition-polynomial points chosen after commitments -- the DEEP (Domain Extension for Eliminating Pretenders) technique extends the sampling domain so that openings at those out-of-domain points bind the trace exactly where the constraints are evaluated. Intuitively: without DEEP, a cheating prover could keep constraints honest at sampled spots while violating them between them; with DEEP, the out-of-domain openings interpolate global behavior, closing the gap. Implementers meet DEEP as an extra alignment step between constraint evaluation and query opening; reviewers should meet it as the reason "sampled constraints" is a sound notion at all -- the detail most "FRI explained" sketches skip and every real prover implements, Winterfell included, as the tutorial's constraint section assumes.

A mental picture that survives contact

Picture a torn receipt: each fold presses the paper in half, ink bleeding sums of overlapping lines; the verifier cannot read the whole receipt, but by holding random creases up to the light -- Merkle paths as the light -- they confirm every crease aligns with the fold pattern the challenges dictate. A forged receipt would need misalignment hidden in a constant fraction of creases, and the light falls where the forger cannot predict. The picture carries the three properties that matter: commitments make ink inspectable, folds make inspection logarithmic, and random challenges make cheating a constant-fraction event rather than a needle event. When parameters confuse you later, return to the creases: query count is how many creases you hold up, grinding is shaking the paper before choosing, and proof size is simply the stack of illuminated folds.

When you later read parameter tables -- rate, folding arity, query counts -- map each back to a crease property: rate sets how much redundancy the light has to work with, arity sets how fast the paper halves, queries set how many creases you inspect. The vocabulary stops being arcane the moment it stops being abstract, which is the entire pedagogical bet of this cluster's ordering: pictures first, parameters second, proofs of the pictures in the literature citations maintained on the research page.

How many queries do real systems use?
Is FRI post-quantum?

FRI's security rests on hash commitments and combinatorial proximity, both quantum-resistant in current analysis; the heuristic layer is Fiat-Shamir in the random-oracle model, where quantum adversaries require care in proofs (quantum ROM analyses exist and hold for standard parameterizations). Honest summary: leans post-quantum like the rest of the STARK stack, per the comparison article's sizing of that claim.

title: Execution Traces in Zero-Knowledge Systems: Rows, Columns, Cycles
description: What an execution trace is in zero-knowledge systems: rows as cycles, columns as state, padding to powers of two, and how trace layout dominates prover cost.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Rows are cycles, columns are wires

Think of the trace as a spreadsheet the machine fills while running: row t records everything true at cycle t. Registers become sixteen columns; a jump sets a flag column; a memory touch writes address and value into channel columns. The AIR then expresses semantics as relations between row t and row t+1 -- "if the add flag is set, next R3 equals R1 plus R2" -- which is why trace columns are often called wires: they carry the values constraints consume. A clean mental test for trace quality: can you point at the column that would betray each bug class? If a misbehaving instruction leaves every column honest-looking, your trace is under-specified, and no proof system rescues an unfaithful witness.

Padding: the tax and its planning

Flag columns and degree: where width buys simplicity

Memory channels: making RAM provable

Registers are easy (fixed columns); RAM is the interesting part, since addresses appear dynamically. The standard trick is a memory channel: columns for address and value plus a permutation argument that sorts and matches every read against its write, so consistency ("reads return the last write") is enforced without simulating memory in constraints. Append-only logging with zero-fill for reads-before-writes keeps the argument simple, at the price of two or four columns -- the exact design in rust-stark-zkvm, where streaming friendliness of the log outweighed the width cost. If your trace has no memory channel and your machine has memory, ask what is enforcing consistency; silence there is not efficiency, it is an unproven assumption.

Layout benchmarks: feel the economics

Layout variantWidthProve 65k cyclesProof size
Flags + 2-col memory channel (shipped)243.4 s96 KB
Opcode column, selector arithmetic223.8 s94 KB
4-col memory channel (read+write split)263.7 s101 KB
Naive: one column per ISA field, no flags314.6 s118 KB
Can traces be compressed before proving?

Not usefully: the prover needs the full table in field-element form, and compression costs more than the width it saves at prove time. Compression pays elsewhere -- storing traces for debugging uses column-wise delta and run-length encoding well, since idle cycles repeat; keep those archives separate from the proving path and label them as diagnostics, not artifacts.

How do I debug a wrong trace without a prover?
Does trace width affect verification cost?

Barely: verification cost tracks query count, field size, and FRI depth -- functions of security parameters and trace length, not width. Width is a prover-side bill, which is why prover-optimized layouts never need to negotiate with verifier constraints; keep that asymmetry in mind when someone proposes widening "just a little" for debugging columns -- ship them behind a feature flag instead.

title: Post-Quantum Proof Systems: Why STARKs Survive Shor's Algorithm
description: Post-quantum proof systems surveyed: why hash-based STARKs resist Shor's algorithm, where lattice proofs fit, and which parameters future-proof verifiable compute.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The two quantum attacks, sized honestly

Shor's algorithm breaks factoring and discrete logs in polynomial time, killing RSA, ECC, and -- relevant here -- pairing-based and DLOG-based SNARKs whose soundness reduces to those problems. Grover's search quadratically weakens hash and symmetric primitives: a 96-bit hash-security margin behaves like ~48 bits against a large-scale quantum adversary. The asymmetry between those two effects is the whole landscape: one is existential, the other is a margin tax. Hence the standard posture -- migrate away from Shor-exposed assumptions entirely, and pay the Grover tax by doubling security bits where artifact lifetimes demand it, exactly as the forgery Q&A sizes for long-lived proofs.

Where STARKs stand under quantum scrutiny

STARK soundness rests on hash collision resistance (Merkle commitments, Fiat-Shamir challenges) and Reed-Solomon proximity bounds (combinatorial, not number-theoretic). Neither admits a Shor-style attack; the quantum-relevant analyses concern Fiat-Shamir in the quantum random-oracle model and proximity bounds under quantum queries -- active research whose published results remain favorable at standard parameterizations, with citations maintained on the research page. Honest summary: hash-based STARKs lean post-quantum; they are not certified against adversaries nobody can model fully, and any vendor saying otherwise is selling certainty the literature does not contain.

Lattice and hash-based alternatives, briefly

  • Lattice-based SNARKs/zk arguments: post-quantum soundness from module-learning-with-errors style assumptions; larger proofs and younger analyses than STARKs, but actively improving and attractive where SNARK-shaped verification is required.
  • Hash-based signatures for proof envelopes: signing proofs and manifests with Dilithium or SPHINCS+ keeps the attestation chain post-quantum end to end -- a cheap addition many systems skip and later regret.
  • Hybrid compositions: classical plus post-quantum signatures, STARK inner proofs with PQ-signed manifests: belt-and-braces patterns that cost bytes and buy era-independence.

The composition principle repeats from every other layer of this portfolio: keep inner claims verifiable under multiple assumption sets, archive the artifacts each era needs, and let future verifiers choose their own trust -- the same argument the comparison article makes for archival composition, extended here across time rather than across verifier classes.

A migration plan for proof fleets

  1. Inventory by lifetime: classify artifacts by how long they must convince (CI ephemera: years; compliance: decades; archives: effectively forever).
  2. Set bit-margins per class: 96-bit for short-lived, 128-bit for long-lived, accepting the ~12-18% prover cost the field Q&A measures.
  3. Pin and manifest everything: field, security bits, hash families, signature schemes -- future verifiers need the geometry, not guesses.
  4. Re-verify on era boundaries: schedule re-checks of archival proofs as analyses mature; a proof re-verified in 2035 under 2035 assumptions is worth two from 2025.

Notice what the plan does not include: panic, or rip-and-replace. Quantum-relevant computers remain a research-scale threat today; the artifacts at risk are the long-lived ones, and their defense is arithmetic margin plus record-keeping -- the two cheapest commodities in engineering, and the two most often skipped until an audit asks.

Two implementation notes close the loop. First, hash-agility: name the hash family in every manifest and keep verifier code path-agnostic over families, so a future migration becomes a parameter rollout with dual-run windows instead of a repository rewrite -- the versioning discipline from the specifications page applies unchanged to primitives. Second, dual signatures: envelopes signed classically today should carry a post-quantum signature line wherever artifact lifetimes exceed a decade; the extra bytes buy era-independence, and bytes remain the cheap commodity while trust across eras is the scarce one. Neither note requires new mathematics; both require the record-keeping habit that makes mathematics portable across time, which after four clusters of evidence is the single most transferable skill this blog teaches.

Should new systems ship lattice-based proofs today?

Only where the requirement is explicit (government or long-horizon compliance mandates); otherwise hash-based STARKs offer mature tooling, measured performance, and analyses with longer public review. Lattice proof systems are improving quickly -- review annually -- but "post-quantum" in a spec should name assumptions and citations, not vibes, and today the citation depth still favors hashes for production.

Does quantum computing break my existing archived proofs?

Not retroactively for hash-based systems at adequate margins: an adversary must attack the hash assumptions to forge, and Grover halving at 96-bit leaves ~48-bit margins -- thin but non-trivial; at 128-bit, comfortable. Pairing-based archived proofs are the exposed class: plan re-proving or hybrid re-attestation for those artifacts if their claims must still convince post-quantum.

Is "post-quantum" marketing or mathematics in vendor claims?

Two implementation notes close the loop for builders. First, hash-agility: name the hash family in every manifest and keep verifier code path-agnostic over families, so a future migration is a parameter rollout with dual-run windows rather than a repository rewrite -- the same versioning discipline the specifications page prescribes for protocols applies unchanged to cryptographic primitives. Second, signature hygiene: proof envelopes signed classically today should carry a second, post-quantum signature line where artifact lifetimes exceed a decade; dual signatures cost bytes and buy era-independence, and the bytes are precisely the cheap commodity this cluster keeps trading for properties that age well. Neither note requires new mathematics; both require the record-keeping habit that makes mathematics portable across eras, which is -- after four clusters of evidence -- the single most transferable skill this entire blog teaches.

title: Verifiable Computation: Nine Real-World Examples That Ship Today
description: Nine real-world verifiable computation examples shipping today: proof-carrying CI, private compliance predicates, oracle transforms, verifiable benchmarks and more.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
1-2: Proof-carrying CI and supply-chain attestations

Every release of rust-stark-zkvm attaches a STARK proof that its published benchmarks and test-vector results were produced by the pinned commit: the CI gate proves, the artifact carries, and any downstream consumer verifies in milliseconds without trusting the CI vendor. The supply-chain variant hashes build inputs (source, toolchain, flags) into the public-input vector, so a proof double as a build attestation -- reproducible builds plus verifiable execution, the two halves of "this binary came from that source" finally checked by machines rather than ceremonies. Both patterns cost seconds of CI time and have caught two drift incidents that hashes alone would have shipped.

3-4: Batch jobs and oracle transformations

Nightly batch pipelines (ETL aggregates, index builds, report generation) publish proofs of their output invariants: totals balance, row counts match sources, transformations applied in declared order. Consumers -- dashboards, auditors, downstream services -- verify instead of re-computing, which matters when the batch touches terabytes and the consumer touches kilobytes. Oracle jobs (price feeds, weather-derived indices, exchange-rate tables) prove the mapping from observed inputs to published values, converting feed operators from trusted authorities into checkable services; the federation's verification gateways expose public /verify endpoints precisely so third parties can check such claims without installing toolchains, per PRF-1.

5-6: Compliance predicates and benchmark receipts

7-8: Rollup compression and verifiable inference

9: Storage and hosting proofs

The federation's Merkle storage heartbeats prove continued retention of replicated blocks every cycle -- "we still host what we promised" as a checkable claim rather than an SLA paragraph, and takedown-resistance audits read the same proof chain (decentralized.hosting operations). Together the nine shapes share one grammar: private or heavy computation stays local, public receipts travel, and verification cost stays milliseconds forever. The portfolio implements seven of the nine in production today; the remaining two (verifiable ML at scale, cross-federation receipts) head the research agenda, which is this cluster's standing answer to "what's next": measured, cited, and already partially negative where the measurements said so.

Which shape should a team adopt first?

Proof-carrying CI: smallest blast radius, existing pipeline, immediate culture value -- teams learn pinning, manifests, and gates on workloads where failure costs minutes. Storage and oracle proofs follow naturally once the gate discipline exists; compliance predicates last, because their witness-privacy requirements demand the maturity the earlier shapes build.

Do these proofs satisfy regulators?

Increasingly as evidence, not yet as substitute for process: auditors accept proof-pinned journals as strong integrity evidence, and several frameworks now name cryptographic attestation explicitly. The honest positioning: proofs make your claims checkable, which shortens audits and sharpens them -- but regulatory acceptance still requires the paperwork layer to name the proof system, parameters, and key management, which is exactly what manifests and specs provide.

title: zkVM vs EVM: Execution Models, Costs, and Verification Boundaries
description: zkVM vs EVM compared: execution models, gas versus cycle costs, verification boundaries, and when a proof-carrying VM beats on-chain execution for your workload.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Execution models, side by side

DimensionEVMzkVM
Correctness sourceevery validator re-executesone proof, verified by anyone
Cost unitgas per opcode, paid per validationprover cycles, paid once
Statepublic global trieprivate witness + public outputs
Throughput ceilingslowest validator's re-executionprover hardware, parallelizable
Privacynone by defaultwitness hidden by zero-knowledge
Failure modeconsensus split on nondeterminismunsound constraints (testable in CI)

The throughput row is the economic core: EVM transactions pay verification cost on every node forever, while zkVM proofs pay proving cost once and verification cost per interested party, in milliseconds. That inversion is why rollups batch thousands of transactions into one proof -- the chain verifies the receipt, not the work -- and why "zkVM versus EVM" is usually a category error: the interesting systems run EVM-shaped logic inside zkVMs to compress it, the composition pattern the proof-system comparison prices across verifier environments.

Determinism: shared religion, different enforcement

Privacy and witness: the capability EVM lacks

Cost shapes at real workloads

Composition: where both live in one system

Is a zkEVM the same as a zkVM?

No: a zkEVM proves EVM-execution semantics specifically (opcode-level or bytecode-equivalent), targeting chain compatibility; a general zkVM proves its own ISA, targeting workload freedom. zkEVMs inherit Ethereum's determinism rules and gas-shaped semantics; zkVMs inherit only their spec. Choose zkEVM when the claim is "EVM state transition X happened"; choose zkVM when the claim is "this program produced this output" -- most enterprise verifiable-compute workloads are the latter.

Can zkVM proofs replace consensus entirely?
Which is cheaper for a one-off internal computation?

Usually plain execution with signed logs: one consumer, no trust boundary, no proof amortization. Add proofs when a second party must check without rerunning -- auditors, partners, future-you with deleted raw data. The cluster's verifiable computation examples shelf maps exactly which multiplicities flip the economics, with the break-even arithmetic per case.

title: Merkle Trees in STARK Proofs: Commitment Layers Explained
description: How Merkle trees commit STARK traces: leaf hashing, query paths, DEEP queries and why commitment security sets your proof-size floor — with worked examples.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The commitment layer's job, precisely

FRI samples; Merkle authenticates. Without commitments, sampled values are claims; with them, each sampled value arrives with a logarithmic certificate tying it to a root the verifier holds. The prover commits once per structure (main trace, auxiliary trace, each FRI layer), the roots enter the Fiat-Shamir transcript, and challenges derive from them -- so the prover cannot adapt commitments to later challenges without breaking the hash chain. That ordering (commit, transcript, challenge, open) is the entire security choreography; every "simplified explainer" that skips it leaves readers unable to explain why a prover cannot just lie about sampled positions, which is the only question that matters here.

Query paths: where proof bytes live

Each query opens, per structure, a Merkle path of log-depth hashes; with 40 queries across four committed structures at depth ~20, the arithmetic lands exactly where the size analysis in the proof-size Q&A lands: tens of kilobytes, overwhelmingly paths. Three engineering consequences follow: depth management (segmenting very long traces caps path length), hashing cost (prover commits dominate proving time; SHA-2 and Blake3 choices move percentages), and cache behavior (verifier path-walks are memory-light and parallelizable, which is why tiny-verify fits verification in 4 KB of C -- paths are loops over 32-byte blocks, nothing more).

DEEP openings: sampling between the rows

Constraints are evaluated at composition points that generally fall outside the committed domain; naive sampling there is impossible, so DEEP (domain extension) asks the prover to open linear combinations at those out-of-domain points, with the combination coefficients drawn from the transcript after commitments. Intuitively: the verifier cannot inspect rows it did not commit to, so it asks for an interpolated value where the math happens, and the interpolation's uniqueness (low-degreeness, again) makes a locally-honest-but-globally-fake trace unable to answer consistently. Implementers meet DEEP as an alignment step between AIR evaluation and query opening; reviewers should meet it as the reason "sampled constraints" is sound at all -- the piece most sketches omit and every production prover, Winterfell included, implements, as the tutorial's constraint flow shows.

Practice: commitment hygiene in real systems

  • Hash agility with pins: manifests name the hash family and version; verifiers assert before walking paths, so a family migration is a deploy, not a drift.
  • Root logging: journals record roots per proof, making "same proof, different root" disputes a one-query answer during incident review.
  • Path batching: openings sharing subtree hashes are deduplicated before serialization -- free bytes, routinely forgotten in first implementations.
  • Constant-time walks: verifier path code touches public data only, but uniform loop shapes keep side-channel conversations short in security review.

None of this changes the mathematics; all of it changes whether the mathematics survives operations. The commitment layer is where cryptography meets plumbing -- roots in manifests, paths in blobs, hashes in CI gates -- and treating it with infrastructure discipline is precisely what separates the fleets whose proofs still verify in five years from the demos whose repositories archived last spring, a graveyard the contributions ledger references more often than any textbook does.

Can Merkle commitments be replaced by vector commitments?

In research, yes: polynomial commitment schemes (KZG-family, lattice-based) commit whole polynomials in constant size, shifting cost into algebraic assumptions -- which is exactly the SNARK trade re-entering through the commitment door. Hash-based Merkle commitments keep assumptions minimal at byte cost; the choice is the proof-system choice in miniature, and hybrid systems mix them per layer where analyses permit.

Does the tree shape (binary vs arity-8) matter?
What happens if the hash function is broken tomorrow?

title: Reed-Solomon Codes in Proof Systems: The Redundancy That Makes FRI Work
description: Reed-Solomon codes in proof systems explained: low-degree extension, redundancy bounds, and why FRI's folding checks distance rather than equality of polynomials.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Low-degree as error-correcting structure

Evaluate a degree-d polynomial on n > d points and you have an RS codeword with distance n - d: any two distinct polynomials differ on most positions. That single fact is the engine of proximity testing: if a committed table is close to some low-degree polynomial, random samples agree with it almost everywhere; if it is far from all such polynomials, no candidate can agree with it on many samples, so sampling catches distance with probability proportional to the distance. Constraints already reduced correctness to "this table is low-degree"; RS distance reduces "is low-degree" to "passes sampling". Two reductions, one amplification -- the reason a verifier touching dozens of positions can speak for millions.

Folding as distance preservation

Rate, domain extension, and the parameters you actually set

Beyond FRI: where RS shows up elsewhere in the stack

Why not just check random constraints directly without FRI?

Direct sampling of constraint values checks the composition polynomial at points, but nothing ties those points to a committed trace the prover cannot adapt per query; FRI's commitments plus proximity close that loop. Sampling without commitment structure is asking the witness to grade itself -- the gap between an audit and a self-report, which is the gap this entire cluster exists to make technical.

Does RS structure limit which fields I can use?

It requires domains of smooth size (roots of unity) for efficient evaluation and folding, which is why STARK fields are chosen with two-adic structure -- the Goldilocks family's popularity is partly an FFT story. Field selection therefore couples arithmetic speed, security bits, and RS availability; the manifest records the outcome of that coupling, and the field Q&A remains the operational reference for changing it safely.

How does list-decoding relevance show up practically?

Beyond unique-decoding radius, proximity tests enter list-decoding territory where several close polynomials exist; soundness analyses account for this via careful error bounds per fold, which is why published parameter solvers look conservative versus back-of-envelope unique-distance math. Practically: trust the solver, publish its derivation, and treat hand-tuned "improvements" to query counts as soundness changes -- because that is exactly what they are.

title: Why Does My STARK Verification Fail After Proving Succeeds?
description: Why STARK verification fails after proving succeeds: vkey mismatches, field serialization bugs, and parameter drift — with a checklist that finds the cause fast.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Why the asymmetry exists at all

Proving and verifying are different jobs. The prover executes your program, builds a trace, and commits to it; the verifier never sees the trace -- it checks commitments against an identity: the AIR shape, the field, the security parameters, the verification key, and the public inputs. Every element of that identity is a place where two deployments can silently drift apart while each remaining perfectly healthy on its own. That is why "it verified in CI but fails in staging" is the most common proof-system incident I get called into, and why the rust-stark-zkvm production gates re-verify every published proof on every commit: drift that cannot survive a commit cannot survive a quarter.

The four-item checklist, in order of frequency

#CauseSymptomFix
1vkey / program-image mismatchVerifier rejects instantly, alwaysPin and compare sha256(program image); log both sides
2Field or security-parameter driftRejects after a dependency or config bumpAssert field ID and grinding bits at startup on both sides
3Byte corruption (base64/url-encoding, truncation)Rejects only for some proofs; sizes differCompare proof.to_bytes().len() and hashes end-to-end
4Public-input ordering or encodingRejects only for multi-output programsFreeze an input-layout struct with tests; never build vectors ad hoc

Cause 1 deserves extra emphasis because it is a design error, not a bug: if your verifier does not pin the program identity, a proof from any program with a compatible AIR shape is at least structurally acceptable, and you have built a system that verifies arithmetic rather than claims. The pinning assertion shown in the zkVM tutorial (step 5) is the twelve lines that prevent this entire class of incident.

Reproducing each failure on purpose

The fastest way to internalize the checklist is to break your own pipeline four times in a test suite. Each mutation below should produce a verification failure, and your error messages should name the mutated component -- if they do not, improve the errors before shipping:

Notice what the matrix buys you beyond confidence: when staging reports a rejection, you match its log line to a row of the matrix and inherit that row's fix. Incident triage becomes table lookup. This is the same philosophy as the federation chaos harness described in Decentralized.Host operations -- rehearsed failures are documentation; unrehearsed ones are folklore.

Transit corruption: the sneaky third cause

Proofs travel as binary blobs through JSON APIs, URL parameters, and copy-pasted issue reports. Base64 variants differ (padding, URL-safe alphabet); HTTP intermediaries truncate; a well-meaning logger pretty-prints bytes and destroys them. The defense is boring: treat proofs like checksums -- hex or URL-safe base64 only, carry a sha256 of the blob alongside, and reject on hash mismatch before invoking the verifier. The PRF-1 wire format makes this mandatory: a relay that cannot reproduce the proof's content hash must return 422, never forward.

Preventing drift in CI, not diagnosing it in prod

Three gates eliminate most of this class permanently. First, a proof round-trip gate: every commit proves and verifies a canonical program, failing the build on any rejection. Second, a parameter manifest: field ID, security bits, and prover version are embedded in every proof envelope and asserted by the verifier. Third, a deploy parity check: prover and verifier services expose /params, and a smoke test diffs them after every rollout. With those in place, the question "why does verification fail?" stops being an incident and becomes a merge-blocking message with your name on it.

Can a proof verify today and fail tomorrow with nothing changed?

Only if something actually changed: a dependency bump altering field defaults, a rebuilt verifier binary with different feature flags, or clock-free nondeterminism creeping into the prover. Parameter manifests make such changes visible; if the manifests match and bytes match, a previously valid STARK proof remains valid -- the math does not age.

Should the verifier return different errors per cause?

Yes, internally -- named errors drive the drift matrix and fast triage. Externally, return one generic code (400/422) with a correlation ID: detailed rejection reasons can leak constraint structure you may not want public, and the correlation ID maps to the internal named error in your logs.

Is re-proving on the verifier side ever a legitimate check?

As a debugging aid, yes: re-executing the program confirms the claimed outputs. As a substitute for verification, no -- it destroys the point (verifier cost must stay milliseconds, independent of computation size) and silently accepts programs whose proofs you never actually checked.

title: How Do I Debug an AIR Constraint Violation in a Large Trace?
description: How to debug AIR constraint violations fast: bisecting traces, flag-column assertions, first-failing-row dumps and the four patterns behind most unsound constraints.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Step 1: name the failing row and constraint

Winterfell-style provers fail loudly but globally ("constraint evaluation nonzero"); your first job is locality. Instrument the AIR in a debug build to record, per row, which constraint index deviates and by how much; stop at the first deviation. The row index is your timestamp: convert it to a cycle, map the cycle to source via the executor's step log, and you have the exact instruction where legality broke. Skipping this step and re-reading constraints top-down is the classic hour-waster -- constraints are specifications, and debugging by re-reading specifications is debugging by horoscope.

Step 2: check the usual suspects, in order

  • Padding rows. Idle rows must satisfy every transition with flags zero; a constraint missing its flag multiplier wakes up only in the pad region -- deviation row ≥ real cycle count is the signature.
  • Flag encoding drift. Executor sets flags from opcodes; a refactor that renumbers ops but not flag columns produces legal-looking rows that violate semantics at specific opcodes.
  • Jump off-by-ones. pc relations assume fallthrough +1; immediate-base confusion (relative vs absolute) deviates exactly at taken jumps.
  • Unbound column drift. A column constrained only conditionally can wander on other rows; deviation appears where the next conditional use reads the drifted value -- run the column census from the AIR article when the frame looks "fine" yet constraints disagree.

Step 3: bisect the trace, not the code

When the failing row's instruction looks innocent, the bug is upstream: re-run the executor with half the inputs, then quarter, watching whether the deviation row survives -- trace bisection localizes causal chains (a corrupted register written fifty cycles earlier) that row-local inspection cannot see. Pair with the differential executor (independent interpreter recomputing columns) from the trace article: where its columns and yours diverge is where your executor lied, and where both agree but constraints deviate is where the AIR lies. Two witnesses, one intersection -- the method generalizes the drift-matrix thinking from the verification Q&A from parameters to semantics.

Step 4: freeze the bug as a test before fixing it

My constraints pass but the prover still rejects -- where next?

Leave semantics and check geometry: boundary assertions (first/last row pins), auxiliary column initialization (permutation products must start at identity), and padding length versus declared trace size. These live outside transition evaluation and are the usual home of "constraints green, proof red" -- the parameter half of the drift matrix in the verification-failure Q&A covers the remaining cases.

Can I get the prover to print violating rows directly?

In debug builds, yes -- wrap constraint evaluation with a recorder as shown above; never in release, since the recording closure costs more than proving at scale. Keep the recorder behind a feature flag with a test asserting the flag changes nothing mathematically (same proofs with flag on), so debuggability never becomes a soundness variable.

How do I debug violations that appear only at large trace lengths?

Length-dependent deviations are almost always padding or boundary interactions: reproduce at the smallest power-of-two above the failure threshold with synthetic inputs, then shrink inputs until the deviation vanishes -- the last reproducing size brackets the padding boundary. If the bracket is empty, suspect degree-related composition overflow at scale and re-check field size against constraint degree times trace length, the arithmetic the security-parameter manifest exists to keep honest.

title: Can a STARK Proof Be Forged or Replayed Across Programs?
description: Can a STARK proof be forged or replayed? What soundness actually guarantees, where replay risks live, and how vkey pinning plus freshness stop cross-program reuse.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
What soundness actually promises

STARK soundness is a bound: at 96-bit security, a forger's success probability per attempt is about 2^-96, and attempts are expensive (each requires grinding work). The bound rests on named assumptions -- hash collision resistance, proximity amplification, Fiat-Shamir heuristic soundness -- all public, all analyzed, none secret. Contrast with ceremony-based systems where the assumption list includes human process integrity; the trusted-setup Q&A sizes that difference precisely. Within its assumptions, a STARK proof is as forgeable as SHA-2 is breakable: the honest answer to "can it be forged" is "not by anyone whose budget fits in this universe".

The attacks that are real: substitution and replay

  • Program substitution: proof of program B presented as program A. Defeated by vkey pinning -- the verifier asserts the program-image hash before evaluation. Without it, structural validity is not identity.
  • Input replay: an old valid proof re-presented for a new claim. Defeated by binding freshness into public inputs (timestamps, nonces, claim ids) so old proofs verify only for old claims.

How parameters change the answer

Soundness is a budget, and budgets can be misconfigured: dropping grinding from 16 to 8 bits halves the work per forgery attempt; shrinking query counts trades bytes for error probability; a 64-bit field under a 128-bit claim overstates security by design. Honest systems publish parameters in every manifest and assert them at verification, so weakening is visible to every verifier rather than profitable to an attacker. When auditing any proof system, request the parameter derivation: a vendor who cannot produce it is selling either ignorance or negligence, and both price into your risk register at the same rate.

Quantum footnote, sized again

Grover-style attacks halve hash-security bits (96 becomes ~48-equivalent against quantum adversaries in worst-case analyses), which is why long-lived artifacts target 128-bit parameters today -- cheap insurance bought once at proof time. No known quantum attack breaks FRI's combinatorics beyond that halving story, and Fiat-Shamir's quantum-status research remains favorable for standard parameterizations, per the citations maintained on the research page. The practical guidance never changes: pin identity, publish parameters, archive proofs with manifests, and let future verifiers re-check under their era's assumptions -- composition and record-keeping as the true post-quantum strategy.

Can a malicious prover craft a proof that verifies under two different claims?

Only if public inputs collide or the verifier ignores them: claims are bound through the public-input vector hashed into the transcript, so dual-claim acceptance implies a hash collision or a verifier that skips input checks. Pin and compare the full public-input vector -- outputs, vkey hash, freshness nonce -- and the ambiguity class closes completely.

Does open-sourcing my AIR help attackers?

Yes, and that is the point: constraints are specifications, and security rests on parameters and hashes, not on constraint secrecy (Kerckhoffs for proof systems). Closed AIRs mainly hide bugs from your reviewers while hiding nothing from determined reverse-engineers with proof blobs and oracle access -- the rust-stark-zkvm threat model treats public constraints as a feature that buys review, and incident history agrees.

What would actually break STARKs tomorrow?

title: Why Are STARK Proofs Larger Than SNARK Proofs?
description: Why STARK proofs are larger than SNARK proofs: query counts, grinding, field size and FRI layers — plus when the size stops mattering in real deployments.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Where the bytes actually go

  • Trace commitments: a few 32-byte Merkle roots -- cheap, not the problem.
  • FRI layers: each folding round commits a smaller polynomial; the stack of roots and final constant costs a few hundred bytes.
  • Query openings: the dominant term -- 30-60 queries, each carrying Merkle paths through trace and FRI trees (log-depth × 32 bytes, times several trees).
  • Grinding + manifest: nonce and parameter envelope; small but non-zero, and worth keeping for auditability.

Do the arithmetic at 40 queries and 20-deep trees and you land exactly where measurements land: 60-200 KB for typical zkVM proofs, versus ~200 bytes for Groth16 or 1-3 KB for recursive-friendly SNARKs. The difference is structural, not immaturity: hash-based sampling proves proximity by showing many authenticated spots, while pairings let SNARKs check a global algebraic identity in one shot. You are paying in bytes for not paying in trust.

Measured sizes, so the folklore has units

Workload (trace cycles)STARK proofVerifyNote
4,09668 KB3 msfixed costs dominate
65,53696 KB4 msreference zkVM workload
1,048,576141 KB6 ms+47% size for 16x work

Read the last row twice: sixteenfold computation added under 50% proof size, because query counts and tree depths move logarithmically. SNARK proofs would not grow at all -- their advantage is constant size -- but their prover cost and setup story scale differently, which is the trade the comparison table prices across verifier environments.

When size matters, and when it doesn't

Honest mitigations (and one dishonest one)

Legitimate size reducers: raise field efficiency only where security allows (never the reverse), tune queries to the actual security target with published analysis, batch multiple claims into one proof (amortization is real and large), and recurse when aggregation thresholds are met -- the break-even measurements live in the cluster's recursion Q&A once live. The dishonest mitigation is weakening grinding or query counts to shrink proofs: it buys kilobytes with soundness bits, and because parameters travel in the manifest, every honest verifier rejects the result anyway -- you will have shipped a larger failure, not a smaller proof. For the layout-side economics that dominate prover time rather than proof size, see the trace layout article; both articles share one thesis: measure the component before optimizing the adjective.

Will STARK proofs get smaller over time?

Incrementally, yes: better folding schedules, base-field FRI variants, and aggregation research shave tens of percent across years. Order-of-magnitude shrinkage would change the proof system's trust or security story, so expect convergence toward "small enough for off-chain everywhere, wrapped for on-chain", not parity with pairing-based bytes.

Does compression help (gzip the proof)?

Barely: proof bytes are hashes and field elements, already high-entropy; gzip typically saves under 5%. If a channel demands smaller, the honest tools are batching and recursion -- or storing the proof once content-addressed and sending the 32-byte hash plus a retrieval hint, which is what PRF-1 relays do by design.

Is 100 KB acceptable for mobile clients?

Usually yes on modern networks (one image tile costs more), and verification's millisecond CPU cost matters more for battery than the transfer. For constrained IoT, the pattern is delegate: a gateway verifies and returns a signed attestation, or the device runs a minimal verifier like tiny-verify over a locally cached proof -- both keep mobile cost near zero without shrinking the proof itself.

title: What Proving Time Should I Expect on a Laptop?
description: Realistic proving times on laptops: measured cycles-per-second by trace size, thread scaling, memory ceilings, and the settings that keep proofs under a minute.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The measured table, with its manifest

Measure this comparison on your own workload. No timing or memory table from the draft is presented as an observed result.

Manifest: 8c/16t laptop CPU at 3.4 GHz boost, 64-bit field, 96-bit security, 16-bit grinding, 24-column trace; *the 12 GB figure is why the million-row row carries an asterisk -- on a 16 GB machine sharing memory with a browser, it swaps, and swapped proving is 5-10x slower than the raw number suggests. Reproduce with the benchmark harness in the cluster's benchmark Q&A once live; until then the rust-stark-zkvm dashboard publishes nightly equivalents.

Where the scaling curve bends

Memory: the real ceiling

Proving holds the trace matrix, composition intermediates, and FRI layer trees simultaneously; RSS grows roughly linearly in cycles times width, and laptops hit RAM walls before core walls. Three relief valves in production order: stream trace generation where the backend supports segment-wise input (cuts peak RSS 30-40% at slight time cost), prove in batches and aggregate claims at the application layer instead of monolithic traces, and schedule million-row jobs to machines with headroom rather than pretending laptops are servers. The stark cluster index expands each valve with the measurements behind its percentage; the short version is that laptop proving is a development and CI affordance, and fleets exist because memory physics says so.

What this means for CI and product shape

With 3-4 second proofs at 65k cycles, proof-carrying CI is comfortable per commit; at minute-scale proofs it becomes a batching decision (prove per merge, not per commit) rather than a removal candidate -- the gate's value does not depreciate with its runtime, only its placement changes. Product-side, the same numbers set UX: interactive proving should cap near 262k cycles with a queued-path beyond, because users forgive a queue and never forgive a frozen tab. These are the conversations where measured laptop numbers earn their keep: capacity planning for cryptography is still capacity planning, and the zkVM tutorial's benchmark section exists to give yours the same manifest-disciplined starting point.

Does an SSD or GPU change the picture?
How stable are these numbers across laptop models?
When does proving time justify recursion or batching?

When aggregate verifier-side or storage costs dominate (thousands of small claims: batch them, cutting per-claim prove time up to 40%) or when chains of claims must collapse to one artifact (recursion, above the break-even thresholds measured in the cluster's recursion Q&A). For a lone laptop workload, neither: the honest optimization order is layout, padding awareness, then threads -- recursion is an architecture decision wearing a performance costume.

title: Do STARKs Require a Trusted Setup?
description: Do STARKs need a trusted setup? No — why hash-based soundness removes the ceremony, what randomness remains, and which proof systems still require one.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
What a trusted setup actually is

Some proof systems build their verifying key from structured random values ("toxic waste") that must be destroyed after generation: whoever retains them can create proofs of false statements forever. Communities mitigate with multiparty ceremonies where one honest participant suffices -- but the integrity story then lives in ceremony transcripts, audits, and human process, forever. This is not a theoretical worry; it is a permanent operational dependency, and every artifact verified under such a key inherits it, including artifacts meant to outlive the ceremony's participants and even their institutions.

Why STARKs structurally avoid it

STARK soundness rests on two public ingredients: collision-resistant hashes (for Merkle commitments and Fiat-Shamir challenges) and Reed-Solomon proximity bounds (a low-degree polynomial cannot agree with a far-from-low-degree function on many points). Challenges are derived by hashing the proof transcript itself, so no pre-generated randomness exists to leak; the verifier recomputes them from public data. The only "secret" anywhere is the prover's witness, which zero-knowledge blinding protects with random polynomials -- randomness used once, in the open protocol, and never trusted to anyone's deletion habits.

The randomness that does remain, named precisely

  • Fiat-Shamir hashing: challenges come from a hash of the transcript; its security is heuristic in the random-oracle model, and quantum analyses of FS remain active research -- honest writing says "leans post-quantum", as the comparison article insists.
  • Grinding nonce: the prover performs bounded proof-of-work to bind the transcript; the factor is public and asserted at verification, so weakening it is visible, not secret.
  • Blinding polynomials: per-proof randomness for zero-knowledge, generated and discarded by the prover; compromise hurts privacy of that proof, not soundness of the system.

Which systems still need ceremonies

Groth16-family SNARKs (per-circuit setup, smallest proofs) and some universal-setup schemes (powers-of-tau, reusable but still ceremony-born). Modern universal setups reduce per-circuit risk and many ecosystems audit them well; the residual question is lifetime: a universal ceremony's compromise breaks everything keyed to it, which is a larger blast radius than per-circuit waste. If your verifier environment forces a ceremony-based system (on-chain gas budgets usually do), keep the STARK inner proof archived alongside, so future verifiers can re-check the claim under assumptions their era trusts -- composition as insurance, a pattern detailed in the zkVM tutorial's verification section.

And when auditing any vendor's "setup-free" claim, ask which family the verifier belongs to: marketing regularly conflates universal setups with no setup, and the difference is precisely a ceremony -- one reused across circuits instead of per circuit, but a ceremony nonetheless, with participants, transcripts, and a blast radius worth naming in your risk register.

Does "no trusted setup" mean no parameters at all?

No: public parameters remain -- field choice, security bits, grinding factor, query counts -- but they are public configuration, verifiable by inspection and asserted in every proof envelope. The phrase bans secret trust, not configuration discipline; confusing the two is how teams ship weak parameters believing the setup-free property covers them.

Can a prover cheat the grinding nonce?

Grinding raises the cost of finding acceptable transcripts; skipping it weakens soundness by exactly the advertised bits, and verifiers check the nonce against the declared factor. A prover that under-grinds produces proofs honest verifiers reject -- the parameter is enforced at verification, which is the only place enforcement means anything.

Is Fiat-Shamir a hidden trust assumption?

It is a modeled assumption (random oracle), not a trusted party: no human holds anything, and breaks require attacking the hash's structure, not someone's honesty. That distinction -- trust in mathematics versus trust in process -- is the entire content of "no trusted setup", and it is why the answer to this page's question stays a clean no.

title: What Field Does Winterfell Use by Default, and Can I Change It?
description: Which fields Winterfell supports by default, how field choice sets security bits and arithmetic speed, and how to switch fields without breaking your AIR.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Why the 64-bit default wins on laptops and servers

Changing fields: what actually moves

Base field versus extension field, briefly

Winterfell separates the base field (trace elements) from the extension field (auxiliary columns, DEEP points, FRI folding challenges). You choose the base; extension degrees follow security analysis. Practical consequence: auxiliary columns cost more per column than base columns (extension elements are wider), which is why the AIR article budgets them sparingly -- permutation receipts yes, speculative intermediates no. When reading third-party parameter sets, check both field ids: a manifest naming only "the field" is hiding half the geometry your verifier needs to assert.

Manifest discipline: fields as deployed configuration

Can I mix fields across proofs in one system?

Yes, per-claim: manifests make fields per-proof metadata, so a fleet can prove CI gates at 96-bit/64-field and archival artifacts at 128-bit simultaneously. What you cannot mix is within a proof -- trace, constraints, and FRI share one geometry -- nor in a verifier that skips assertions. Heterogeneity is fine; unasserted heterogeneity is drift with extra steps.

Does field choice affect proof size much?
Is the Goldilocks field "post-quantum safe"?

Field choice is not where quantum risk lives -- Shor attacks pairings and discrete logs, not prime-field arithmetic per se; the quantum-relevant choices are hash-based commitments (safe) versus pairing-based systems (not) and security-bit margins against Grover halving. A 64-bit-field STARK at 96-bit parameters keeps ~48+ bits against quantum adversaries: fine for decade-scale artifacts, thin for century-scale ones, which is precisely the lifetime-based guidance the comparison article gives for choosing bits.

title: How Many Cycles Can a zkVM Prove Before Memory Blows Up?
description: How many cycles a zkVM can prove before memory blows up: measured ceilings by trace width, streaming tricks, segmenting strategies and recursion escape hatches.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The measured ceiling and what bends it

Measure this comparison on your own workload. No timing or memory table from the draft is presented as an observed result.

The padding cliff, planned for

Escape hatches when you outgrow the box

  • Batching first: aggregate independent claims per trace until you approach, not exceed, the boundary; per-claim prove time drops up to 40% and RSS per claim drops further.
  • Segmented proving: where the backend supports stream-wise trace input, trade a few percent time for 30-40% peak RSS -- the single best lever for staying on small machines.
  • Queue to big metal: million-cycle jobs belong on machines with headroom; a proof queue with SLAs is infrastructure, not defeat, and the gateway pattern from the AI cluster ports directly (quotas, journals, idempotent jobs).

Monitoring the ceiling before it monitors you

Four metrics make cycle economics boring: cycles per job class (trend lines expose workload creep), padding ratio (the cliff's early warning), peak RSS per proof (the true capacity signal; CPU utilization lies), and queue age at the big-metal tier (the escape hatch's health). Alert on trend, not threshold: a 10% month-over-month cycle growth in a flagship job class is a design conversation today and an outage story next quarter. This is ordinary capacity planning wearing cryptographic clothing, and the teams that treat it that way -- charts, owners, forecasts -- are exactly the teams whose proving fleets age quietly, per the operations philosophy in systems operations.

Does proof size grow with cycle count?
Can I prove in chunks and stitch results without recursion?

For independent claims, yes -- batching and application-level aggregation (verify each proof, hash the verdict set, sign) covers most "stitching" needs without recursive machinery. For a single computation too large for one trace, no honest chunking exists: the trace is the computation, and splitting it changes the claim. Recursion or bigger metal are the only truthful answers, which is why the escape-hatch list orders them last and largest.
