CloudflareZone:DNS edit, one zoneAccount-wide tokens also edit billing-adjacent settings
Route53IAM: changeResourceRecordSets on one hosted zoneWildcard IAM on route53:* is the classic overgrant
deSEC / PowerDNSPer-zone API token (native)None notable -- prefer providers with native zone scoping
GoDaddy et al.Account-level DNS token (no zone scope)Token compromises every zone you own; isolate the domain

Where a provider cannot scope to a zone, scope the domain: register the self-hosting identity on its own domain with its own registrar account, so a leaked token burns one zone instead of your portfolio. Store tokens in your secrets manager (never in the renewal script), rotate annually, and log every use -- the audit trail doubles as renewal monitoring, since a token that stops working shows up as a missing log line before it shows up as an expired certificate.

Propagation waits: bounded, observable, patient

DNS is eventually consistent by design; your renewal job must be eventually patient. The pattern that never wakes me: after writing the TXT, poll an external resolver (not the provider's own nameservers) every 10 s with a 180 s budget; on timeout, abort loudly rather than letting the CA time out opaquely. Multi-vantage checks matter for split-horizon zones: your LAN resolver may answer from cache while the CA's validators see nothing. If your provider's propagation is routinely slow, pre-create a long-TTL _acme-challenge CNAME to a fast-scoped zone -- the indirection buys you both speed and a token surface you actually control.

Renewal timers that survive reboots, redeploys, and you

Three rules finish the job: renew at 30 days remaining (not 24 hours -- propagation plus one failed attempt needs runway); make the reload command idempotent and tested (a renewal that fetches a cert but never reloads the web server is a 30-day-delayed outage); and alert on the absence of success -- a heartbeat metric per domain into whatever monitoring the exit guide's substrate month stood up, because certificate incidents announce themselves in browser chrome, politely, to your users first.

Staging first: the rehearsal that costs nothing

Run the entire chain -- issue, propagate, install, reload, verify with openssl s_client -- against the CA's staging environment until it passes twice, then flip one flag. Staging rate limits are generous and its certs are untrusted by design, which is exactly the property you want while a cron typo is still possible. The same discipline applies after any provider API change: staging catches their breaking changes during your office hours. For what to do when the server has no inbound path at all, pair this guide with hosting without a static IP; for wildcard-serving patterns once certs exist, the federation's edge layer in Decentralized.Host documents its DNS-01 automation in the same shape.

Can I use DNS-01 with a self-hosted DNS server instead of a provider?

Yes, and it is the sovereignty-maximal setup: run your own authoritative server (PowerDNS or Knot) with a scoped API, and DNS-01 becomes pure local automation with zero third-party token. The cost is that your DNS server becomes internet-reachable infrastructure -- monitoring, TSIG/API auth, and a secondary somewhere else's network -- so adopt it after, not before, your substrate habits are proven.

Why did renewal succeed but my browser still show the old cert?

Almost always a missing or failed reload step: the cert files changed on disk while the serving process kept the old chain in memory. Verify with openssl s_client against the port, not with the file mtime; then fix the reload command (some servers need restart, not reload, for TLS material) and add a post-renewal check that fails loudly when served and on-disk fingerprints disagree.

Are 90-day certificates going away in favor of shorter ones?

The direction is shorter, not longer: industry roadmaps point toward 45-day and eventually ~10-day public certs, which turns renewal from a quarterly worry into pure automation. Every hour spent making your DNS-01 chain boring, observed, and staging-tested now is future-proofing against that timeline -- manual renewal workflows are already dead; they just haven't stopped moving yet.

title: Reverse Proxy with Automated TLS: Caddy vs Nginx+ACME
description: Reverse proxy with automated TLS: Caddy on-demand HTTPS versus Nginx plus certbot or acme.sh, HTTP/3, headers and the migration order that avoids downtime.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Caddy: the zero-config path, done properly

Caddy's magic is ACME wired into the server lifecycle: certificates obtain at first request, renew before expiry, and reload without downtime. The discipline around the magic is what production adds: origins bound to localhost only (verify with ss -tlnp, the check from the exposure guide), explicit HSTS once you are sure (it is a one-way door per browser), and the DNS-01 plugin configured with the scoped tokens the DNS-01 guide treats as crown jewels. On-demand TLS for multi-tenant edges exists but needs a permission endpoint -- never enable it open to arbitrary hostnames, or your proxy becomes the internet's certificate laundry.

Nginx plus ACME clients: the explicit-control path

Nginx gives you per-directive control and decades of operational literature; the cost is owning renewal yourself. The shape that ages well: certbot or acme.sh with webroot or DNS-01 plugins, systemd timers with Persistent=true (the same persistence argument as backups and certs elsewhere in this cluster), a reload -- not restart -- on renewal so in-flight requests drain, and a config test (nginx -t) inside the renewal hook so a bad template fails the renewal loudly instead of the reload silently. Snippet discipline matters more than directives: one ssl-hardening.conf and one headers.conf included by every server block, versioned in your config repository, because forty copy-pasted server blocks with drifted cipher lists are how "we have TLS" becomes "we have forty TLS configurations".

Headers, protocols, and the edge's real job

  • HSTS after your first clean month; preload only for domains you accept owning forever.
  • HTTP/2 and HTTP/3: on by default in Caddy, one directive in modern Nginx; QUIC needs UDP 443 open and pays off on lossy mobile paths.
  • Compression at the edge for text types only; never compress already-compressed media, and mind BREACH-class thinking on authenticated responses.
  • Client-body limits at the proxy (the same default-body-limit reasoning as the axum tutorial), raised per-route with intent.
  • Logging with request ids propagated to origins via headers, so traces span the edge instead of dying at it.

Migrating edges without downtime

Monitoring the terminator

Watch four things at the edge: certificate expiry per name (external checks, not internal state), TLS handshake errors by version (sudden SNI or protocol anomalies precede client-ecosystem shifts), 5xx ratio per origin (the edge sees origin death before users do), and config-reload success (a failed reload that leaves an old worker fleet serving is a time bomb with a log line). Alert on silence as elsewhere in this cluster: the renewal heartbeat and the reload heartbeat are the two metrics whose absence means your automation died politely. With those green, the edge disappears from your attention entirely -- the correct experience of good termination is never thinking about termination, while the behind-NAT renewal Q&A keeps the certificate half honest in the hardest networks.

Keep one more artifact beside the dashboards: a dated edge-config changelog entry per server block added or removed. Edges accumulate orphan sites the way gardens accumulate weeds, and a quarterly review that deletes dead server blocks shrinks your certificate blast radius and your confusion in the same ten minutes. Ten minutes a quarter, four times a year, forever: the cheapest insurance in this article, and the only policy whose payout you can read in a single diff.

Caddy or Nginx for a homelab in 2026?

Caddy, unless you need a directive Nginx has and Caddy lacks (rare) or your team already speaks fluent Nginx (real). The operational surface you avoid -- renewal hooks, reload choreography, snippet drift -- is exactly the surface where homelabs leak weekends; spend the saved time on restore drills, which protect more than any edge choice.

Should the proxy also be the WAF?

As a first layer, yes-ish: rate limits, body caps, and geo-allowlists at the edge stop commodity noise cheaply. As a security boundary, no: an edge WAF is a smoke detector, not a firewall -- authentication, authorization, and input validation belong in the app or an identity-aware proxy in front of it. Teams that treat ModSecurity-class rules as their security plan maintain rules; teams that treat them as noise-reduction maintain services.

How do I terminate TLS for non-HTTP protocols?

TLS passthrough (SNI routing without termination) for protocols you cannot parse, or the proxy's stream/TCP mode (Nginx stream, Caddy layer4) for termination with client-cert auth where the protocol supports it. Database and broker exposure should still ride the mesh rather than any public edge per the never-open list; passthrough exists for the exceptions that survive that list's review, documented per port like every other policy decision here.

title: Self-Hosted Alternatives to SaaS Tools: 31 Swaps That Stick
description: Thirty-one self-hosted alternatives to SaaS tools that people actually keep using: notes, mail, photos, CRM, analytics and office — with honest swap costs.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Why some swaps stick and others don't

The list, with honest swap costs

  • Notes: Obsidian-over-Syncthing (files stay yours, zero server) or Nextcloud Notes for shared; cost: sync-conflict discipline.
  • Mail: Stalwart or Maddy plus SOGo; cost: deliverability work (PTR, SPF, DKIM, warm-up) -- the one swap where the server is easy and the reputation is the project.
  • Photos: Immich; cost: face-recognition CPU budget and mobile auto-upload tuning; benefit: Google-Takeout-sized imports land in an hour.
  • Passwords: Vaultwarden per the dedicated guide; cost: near zero; benefit: immediate and total.
  • Chat: Matrix/Element; cost: federation optional but tempting, bridge maintenance if you keep old networks.
  • Analytics: Plausible/Umami; cost: losing ad-network integrations you never used anyway.
  • Office: Collabora/OnlyOffice; cost: macro-heavy spreadsheets remain the honest exception -- keep one cloud seat for them and say so.
  • Git/CI: Forgejo + Woodpecker; cost: re-learning pipeline idioms; benefit: runners on your mesh with your secrets.
  • Monitoring: Prometheus trio per the free-monitoring guide; cost: one evening; benefit: every other swap becomes observable.

Migration order that respects weekends

Sequence by reversibility and blast radius: analytics and monitoring first (read-only, zero user impact), then notes and passwords (small data, high habit value), then photos (large data, patient users), then chat (network effects -- migrate groups together or not at all), and mail last, after deliverability homework, with the old account forwarding for a full quarter. Each step ends with the portability checklist from the exit guide signed off: open export verified, restore drilled once, runbook page written. The order's logic is emotional as much as technical: early wins build the household's trust budget, and mail -- the swap most likely to frustrate strangers who email you -- spends from that budget, so it goes last, when the budget is rich.

What I still rent, publicly

How much total time should I budget for all thirty-one?
Which swaps have the worst import tooling?

Mail history (IMAP sync tools vary wildly; budget a test mailbox first) and chat history (export formats are political, not technical). Photos and notes import beautifully almost everywhere, which is why they sit early in the order: your first weekends should taste the good tooling, so the household's morale survives the mail quarter.

Do these swaps survive contact with non-technical family?

The client-first ones do (photos, passwords, notes), because the experience lives in apps they already trust visually. The server-shaped ones (mail, chat federation) survive only with the one-page runbook and a named owner -- non-technical users do not fear self-hosting; they fear unanswered questions at dinner, and the runbook plus owner exists precisely to answer at dinner speed.

title: ZFS Snapshots and Backups Explained: Send, Receive, Scrub
description: ZFS snapshots and backups explained: dataset design, snapshot schedules, incremental send and receive, scrubbing and the restore drills that prove the chain works.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Snapshots: the rollback layer

Snapshots cost nothing until data changes (copy-on-write charges only deltas), which makes hourly cadence cheap and surgical recovery trivial: a file deleted at 14:32 lives in the 14:00 snapshot, retrievable by path without restoring anything else. Automate with sanoid-style retention (hourly 24, daily 7, weekly 4, monthly 6 -- tune to your change rate) and treat snapshot lists as capacity data: growth in snapshot-used space is your churn telemetry, and a sudden spike is often the first symptom of ransomware-shaped activity, worth an alert line beside the security stack's own signals.

Send and receive: the replication layer

zfs send -i prev snap | ssh backup zfs recv pool/mirror transfers only deltas, compressed on the wire, with checksums end to end -- replication as mathematics rather than hope. Production rules: send from a held snapshot (bookmark or sanoid-held) so the incremental base cannot expire mid-stream; receive into a readonly=on destination so nobody edits the mirror into divergence; and verify with periodic zfs get -r checksum-guid comparisons or a received-count dashboard. Raw sends carry encryption keys' ciphertext when the source is encrypted (keep keys escrowed per the exit guide), while non-raw sends decrypt at the source -- choose per threat model and write the choice in the runbook, because "is the mirror readable offline?" has different answers per mode and incidents ask at 3 a.m.

Scrubs: auditing silence

Scrubs read every block against its checksums, repairing silent rot from good parity while the pool is healthy -- the feature that separates ZFS from filesystems that discover rot at read-time panic. Monthly cadence for spinning rust (weekly for pools over five years old or with any SMART whispers), after-hours scheduling (scrubs are IO-heavy), and always check the result: a scrub that found and repaired errors is a saved dataset and a disk on probation; a scrub that cannot repair (insufficient redundancy) is an incident in progress. Log scrub outcomes into the monitoring heartbeats from the monitoring guide: "last scrub clean, 0 errors, 4h12m" is a monthly sentence whose absence should page, because silence from the scrub is indistinguishable from a scrub that never ran.

Drills: where snapshots become backups

Keep one more artifact with the drill log: the receive-side feature-flag matrix (pool features enabled per host generation), because cross-version receives fail on feature gaps more often than on capacity, and a one-line table of pool features per machine converts the year's first cross-generation restore from an error-message excavation into a lookup. The table belongs in the same runbook page as the drill timings -- recovery knowledge co-located is recovery knowledge used, a principle this cluster repeats across clusters precisely because every incident review rediscovers it independently.

Pairing with restic: file-level portability

ZFS replication protects pools and datasets as units; restic from a snapshot mount protects files as units -- cross-platform restores, single-file granularity for non-ZFS destinations, and encrypted repositories that travel to object storage per the offsite guide. Snapshot first, restic from the snapshot mount second: consistent source, zero live-file races, and the snapshot becomes the restore point both layers agree on. The pairing costs one extra timer and removes the last argument in the "ZFS means I don't need backups" debate -- a debate that ends, every time, at the first corruption that predates every snapshot you kept.

How much space do snapshots really cost?

Zero at creation, then churn-proportional: a dataset changing 1% daily costs ~1% of dataset size per daily snapshot until retention prunes it. Model it as dataset size times daily churn times retention days, add 10%, and alert at 80% of the modeled envelope -- snapshot-space surprises are almost always churn surprises (a log directory that joined the dataset uninvited), and the model makes the intrusion visible as arithmetic.

Is RAID-Z1 acceptable for backups pools?

For the backup destination pool, yes with scrubs and smartd watching: its failure mode (second disk death during rebuild) is tolerable when the source pool and offsite restic copies still exist -- redundancy requirements scale with how many copies stand behind a pool. For the only pool holding irreplaceable data, RAID-Z2 or mirrors-plus-offsite is the honest minimum; the topology question is really "how many independent copies exist at every moment", and pools are one answer among several, never the whole answer.

Should I encrypt the pool?

Yes for laptops and any pool whose disks might leave your control (RMA, resale, theft); optional for stationary arrays where the threat model says disks die at home. Encryption adds key management to your escrow obligations -- the envelope gains one more tested artifact -- and slightly narrows some dedupe/replication options; decide per pool, write the decision down, and remember that pool encryption protects stolen disks, not running systems, which attackers and warrants both prefer to meet powered on.

title: Restic Backup Automation Guide: Timers, Pruning, Restore Drills
description: Restic backup automation: systemd timers, repository layout, prune policies, bandwidth caps, health checks and quarterly restore verification you will actually do.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The timer: boring, persistent, jittered

The service unit pairs nice and IO scheduling (Nice=10, IOSchedulingClass=best-effort, IOSchedulingPriority=7) with the bandwidth cap in the restic command itself (--bwlimit 20000 KiB/s, raised off-hours via an EnvironmentFile if your nights are emptier than your days). One unit, one journal stream, one place for on-call to look; wrappers that scatter logic across cron lines and shell history are how backups acquire undocumented branches that fail silently the one night they matter.

Include-lists: fail loud, not silent

Retention: deletion with documented intent

The sentences matter operationally: when someone proposes "keep fewer monthlies to save bytes", the conversation becomes about audit windows rather than vibes, and when a restore request arrives for "the state before March's migration", the yearly tier's existence is a decision already made calmly. Prune runs inside the same unit as backup so retention cannot drift from creation, and --prune repacks concurrently with your bandwidth cap -- uncapped prunes on shared targets are the 3 a.m. network incident nobody scheduled.

Keys, locks, and the paranoia that pays

Repository keys live in your secrets manager and the escrow envelope from the exit guide, never on the backed-up host alone. Where the target supports immutability (B2 object lock, append-only storage-box keys), enable it: ransomware that steals credentials still cannot delete history inside the lock window, converting the worst day into a restore-from-before exercise. Rotate repository passwords annually via restic key add then remove, tested like any drill; and keep one air-gapped or friend-hosted copy on rotation with logged swaps, because two targets under one vendor's jurisdiction is one target wearing a costume, a lesson the offsite Q&A prices in vendor-failure rows.

Monitoring: heartbeats and duration trends

Should backups run on the service host or a puller?
How do I back up running databases consistently?
Is restic dedupe enough to skip compression?

Dedupe kills redundancy across snapshots; compression (--compression max) kills redundancy within files -- text-heavy estates (code, logs, dumps) shrink 2-3x with it, encrypted media not at all. Enable max for document/code repos, auto elsewhere, and measure: the size chart per repository tells you in one week whether compression earned its CPU, which is the only argument either side should bring.

title: Homelab to Production: The 41-Point Checklist I Actually Use
description: A homelab-to-production checklist of 41 points: power, networking, observability, change management, backups, security baselines and the docs future-you needs.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Physical and power (points 1-6)

  • 1. UPS on every stateful box, sized to measured shutdown sequence plus 50% margin.
  • 2. AC-restore plus boot-verification tested by pulling plugs quarterly, per the power-loss Q&A.
  • 3. Thermals logged: intake/exhaust deltas and CPU package temps trended; dust on a calendar, not on a smell.
  • 4. Disk provenance recorded: purchase date, workload rating, SMART baseline at commissioning.
  • 5. Label everything that unplugs: cables, PSUs, UPS outlets -- the 2 a.m. taxonomy problem is real.
  • 6. Spare shelf: one PSU, one boot disk, one data disk class, imaged and ready.

Network and exposure (points 7-12)

  • 7. Management plane (router UI, IPMI, hypervisor) unreachable from WAN -- verified by external scan.
  • 8. Mesh or VPN as the default path in; port forwards are named, dated, reviewed entries.
  • 9. DNS under your control with DNSSEC where the provider allows; wildcard strategy documented per the DNS-01 guide.
  • 10. Edge default-deny ingress; every public hostname has an owner and a purpose line in the edge changelog.
  • 11. Egress filtered per host where feasible; inference and backup hosts egress-deny by default.
  • 12. Network diagram versioned in the config repo, updated in the same commit as topology changes.

Configuration and change (points 13-20)

  • 13. Everything in Git: compose/Nix/Ansible, edge configs, timer units, dashboards-as-code.
  • 14. No edits on boxes: a config change is a commit, a review (even self-review counts written), a deploy.
  • 15. Secrets in a manager, referenced not embedded; rotation dates in the calendar with owners.
  • 16. Deploy path is one command with a dry-run mode and a printed rollback command.
  • 17. Rollbacks rehearsed: each service's rollback executed at least once per year, logged.
  • 18. Version pinning with an update policy: security jumps queue, feature updates ride the monthly window.
  • 19. Boot-from-zero proven: one bare-metal rebuild drill per year from repo plus secrets envelope.
  • 20. Machine-readable inventory: hosts, services, owners, dependencies -- the graph incidents navigate.

Observability and backups (points 21-30)

  • 21-25. The five dashboards and four alerts from the monitoring guide: pressure, disks, heartbeats, network, power; backup/cert/tunnel/ups alerts owned by name.
  • 26. Backup chain: restic offsite plus ZFS receive where pools exist, per the ZFS guide.
  • 27. Weekly automated partial restores with canary diff; quarterly full drills timed and logged.
  • 28. Escrow envelope: secrets, restore procedures, emergency contacts; tested annually with the drills.
  • 29. Log shipping off-box: journals or Loki to the backup target; local logs die with local disks.
  • 30. Uptime probes from outside the LAN see what users see, not what your LAN believes.

Security, docs, and the human layer (points 31-41)

  • 31-34. Security baseline: SSH keys only, unattended security upgrades, WebAuthn on every admin surface, exposure checklist re-run per new service per the exposure guide.
  • 35-37. Docs: one-page runbook per service (restart, rollback, escalate), this checklist printed beside the rack, and a changelog culture where every incident ends with a diff somewhere.
  • 38-39. Humans: named owner per service (households included), successor clause and bus-factor review quarterly per the mentorship philosophy.
  • 40. Maintenance window on the calendar with a standing agenda: updates, drill rotation, orphan pruning, labor-line row.
  • 41. The meta-point: review this checklist quarterly and delete what no longer applies -- a checklist that only grows becomes wallpaper, and wallpaper protects nothing.

Adoption advice from four years: score yourself honestly, fix the power and backup clusters first (points 1-6, 26-29) because they decide whether failures are events or losses, then work outward. Teams and households that reach 35 of 41 with owners named run quieter than most startups' production; the remaining six are usually the honest exceptions -- documented, dated, and accepted, which is what "production" finally means: not perfection, but known shape.

Which points can a solo homelabber skip honestly?

None skipped, several scaled: succession (38-39) becomes the escrow envelope plus one informed relative; review cadences become quarterly instead of monthly; "teams" becomes you-with-a-calendar. The points that must never scale to zero are 1-2 (power), 13-14 (config in Git, no live edits), 27 (restore drills), and 41 (review the list) -- those four are the difference between a homelab and a liability.

How do I introduce this to a resistant team or household?

Start with the drill that scares everyone once (restore one important dataset together), then let the checklist grow from the post-drill conversation -- adopted points stick because they answer a felt wound. Checklist imposition without a shared incident memory produces compliance theater; shared scars produce owners, and owners are the only infrastructure that maintains infrastructure.

Is this checklist compatible with managed cloud hybrids?

Entirely: points map onto cloud controls (UPS becomes AZ design, escrow becomes key management policy, drills become game days). Hybrids should run the checklist per environment with a column noting where the provider owns a point -- the column's emptiness or fullness is your sovereignty metric, and reviewing it annually is exactly the exception-review habit the exit guide prescribes for stayed workloads.

title: Self-Hosted Password Manager Setup: Vaultwarden Done Safely
description: Self-hosted password manager setup with Vaultwarden: hardened deployment, WebAuthn, encrypted exports, client choices and the backup path for your keyring.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Deployment: small, proxied, monitored

SIGNUPS_ALLOWED=false after creating your household accounts removes the discovery-to-spam pipeline entirely; new members join by invitation through the admin console, which itself is bound to /admin and should be reachable only via your mesh or an identity-aware proxy per the exposure guide. Back the container's /data volume with the restic pipeline from this cluster -- the vault database is small, dedupes beautifully, and is the one dataset where restore drills deserve monthly rather than quarterly cadence, because the day you need it is by definition the day everything else is also on fire.

Threat model: what self-hosting changes and doesn't

  • Removed: third-party breach headlines as your incident timeline; vendor policy changes on data retention; subscription as a single point of family lockout.
  • Unchanged: client-side cryptography is the same code Bitwarden ships -- your master password and device hygiene remain the vault; phishing remains the top real-world attack on any password manager.
  • Added: availability is your job (UPS, backups, renewal of the edge cert in front of it), and patching cadence is your policy -- set it monthly with security releases jumping the queue.

The honest summary: you trade diffuse vendor risk for concentrated personal responsibility, exactly the exchange the worth-it analysis prices across services -- and for password managers specifically, the ciphertext-at-rest property makes the personal side unusually winnable, because a compromised server yields encrypted blobs whose keys live only in your household's heads and hardware keys.

Passkeys and 2FA: the layer that saves the vault

Enroll WebAuthn keys (hardware tokens or platform authenticators) for every household admin before inviting anyone else: credential stuffing against your edge is commodity traffic, and a passkey-gated admin console turns it into noise. Per-item practices matter more than server choices for daily safety: unique generated passwords everywhere (the manager's generator, 20+ chars), TOTP inside the vault only for legacy services that lack passkeys, and one documented emergency-access pair (a trusted human with time-delayed emergency access) so the escrow envelope has a human twin. Test emergency access annually like any other restore: an untested delegation is a rumor with a settings page.

Exports, migration, and exit portability

Quarterly, produce an encrypted export (.zip or encrypted JSON) into the escrow envelope and one offsite target; label it with date and vault version. This is the exit-portability clause from the exit guide applied at item granularity: migration to any future manager (self-hosted or otherwise) becomes an import of a standard format rather than a rescue operation, and the envelope covers the catastrophic tier where the server, the backups, and the house are one incident. Keep the export script in your config repository beside the deployment, because a documented export that lives only in someone's memory is a future lockout wearing a backup's costume -- the same lesson the runbook rows teach across this entire cluster.

Label exports with date, vault version, and item count, and verify the count on restore: a silently partial export -- one interrupted attachment, one skipped collection -- is indistinguishable from a complete one until the Sunday it isn't, and a checksummed manifest beside each archive turns that class of surprise into a one-line comparison at drill time.

Vaultwarden versus official Bitwarden server?
Is storing the whole family vault on one box risky?

Concentrated, not risky-by-itself: the ciphertext property means the box holds locked boxes, and your drills plus escrow cover availability while WebAuthn covers access. The genuinely risky family pattern is shared master passwords instead of per-member accounts with org-sharing -- per-member accounts keep revocation (a lost phone, a departed member) a settings change instead of a household rekey weekend.

What breaks first after a year of operation?

One household habit worth stealing regardless of manager: a printed card in the escrow envelope with the vault URL, the export location, and the emergency-access human's phone number -- because the failure mode that actually strands families is not server death but information asymmetry at the worst possible hour, and paper remains the only medium with 100% client compatibility. Review the card annually beside the export -- same envelope, same quarter, same ten minutes as the restore drill -- because a vault whose recovery path is untested is not a vault but a very organized way of losing everything at once, and the entire thesis of this cluster is that organized and verified are different words for a reason: only one of them has ever saved anybody on a bad Sunday.

title: NixOS vs Debian for Home Servers: Reproducibility vs Boring
description: NixOS vs Debian for home servers: reproducibility and rollbacks versus stability and hiring familiarity, with real rebuild times and rescue-disk stories.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
NixOS: reproducibility as operations

Debian: boring as a feature

Debian's advantages are social and logistical: the largest body of home-server tutorials on earth, live-ISO rescue paths every helper recognizes, LTS support windows that outlive hobby enthusiasm, and package availability without derivation detours. For households where the operator might be unavailable (the succession clause from the exit guide), Debian's universality is a resilience property: the neighbor who "knows Linux" knows Debian. Its drift risk -- the /etc edit made at midnight, the package installed ad hoc -- is real but manageable with the same config-repo discipline (Ansible or plain dotfiles plus apt lists in Git), at the cost of enforcing that discipline yourself rather than inheriting it.

Measured differences that matter at home scale

  • Rebuild time: NixOS full rebuild 3-12 min (evaluation plus build, cached thereafter); Debian reprovision from scratch 20-40 min plus your memory of what was installed.
  • Rollback: NixOS generations instant; Debian snapshots possible via filesystem but package-state rollback remains manual archaeology.
  • Upgrade events: NixOS channel/flake bumps are per-change and revertible; Debian release upgrades are biennial projects with read-the-release-notes rituals.
  • Rescue: Debian live ISO plus muscle memory versus NixOS ISO plus config-aware reinstall -- both fine; the difference is who can wield them besides you.

The verdict I give clients, with the hybrid note

Is the NixOS learning curve worth it for one box?

For one box, marginal: the payoff compounds per additional machine and per additional year, since the config repo becomes a library of proven modules. Single-box households should weigh honestly whether they want a second hobby (Nix) inside the first (self-hosting); both are fine hobbies, but name the choice rather than sliding into it via a forum thread at midnight.

Do Debian containers on a NixOS host combine well?

Excellent pairing: host reproducibility plus guest tutorial-compatibility, with the container image versioned beside the host config. The one discipline: never let guest packages satisfy host needs (a Debian cron inside a container doing host backup is a topology lie); keep layers honest and the hybrid's benefits stay additive instead of confusing.

How do secrets work cleanly on NixOS?

sops-nix or agenix: encrypted files in the same repo, decrypted at build/activation with host keys that never leave the machine -- config public, secrets ciphertext, escrow holding the age keys per the household governance pattern. The arrangement makes "public dotfiles" genuinely safe to publish, which changes what you can share with the community, and sharing is how the contribution ledger grew in the first place.

title: Privacy Benefits of Self-Hosting: What Actually Changes
description: What actually changes for privacy when you self-host: telemetry elimination, data locality, warrant realities, metadata leaks you keep, and the threat model shift.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
What actually leaves your threat model

  • Product telemetry and analytics: your services emit what you configure; the default-zero telemetry of self-hosted stacks is a floor no SaaS contract matches.
  • Vendor retention and training use: prompts, files, and metadata stop being subject to someone else's policy changes -- the clause that rewrites itself in ToS emails you never read.
  • Subprocessor chains: the N-deep list of companies touching your data collapses to your hardware and your upstream ISP, both nameable on one line.
  • Aggregation across services: one vendor seeing mail plus calendar plus drive builds a profile no single self-hosted service can, because the integration layer is yours and can be segmented deliberately.

What remains, named without romance

Your ISP still sees traffic volumes, timings, and SNI unless you encrypt at transport (mesh tunnels and TLS everywhere shrink this to metadata about volumes -- meaningful, but smaller). Your endpoints remain the richest attack and leak surface: editor cloud sync, phone backup settings, and browser ecosystems leak more per week than a well-run server leaks per year. And your own operations join the threat model: an exposed port, a default password, an unpatched CVE on your edge is now your incident, with no vendor SOC between you and the scan fleets -- the exposure checklist in this cluster exists because self-hosting converts diffuse vendor risk into concentrated personal responsibility, and concentration cuts both ways.

Measured deltas from my own logs

Privacy as operating practice, not posture

One asymmetry deserves naming for readers weighing this page against a vendor's privacy page: a vendor's privacy improvement arrives as an announcement you must trust, while yours arrives as a diff you can read -- and when your egress audit shows an unexpected flow, the fix ships the same evening without a support ticket, a policy update, or a press cycle. That loop speed is the benefit practitioners feel first and articulate last: privacy engineering at home is not better cryptography than the cloud's (it is usually the same cryptography, worse funded), it is shorter distance between noticing and fixing, with no intermediary's roadmap standing between. Households that internalize this stop comparing themselves to hyperscalers and start comparing themselves to last quarter -- the only comparison a single estate can actually win, and win visibly, on one dashboard row beside the backup heartbeats. Print that row's quarterly history into the household review beside the cost sheet and the restore-drill log; three numbers on one page -- bytes leaving, bytes restorable, hours practiced -- constitute the entire sovereignty report card, and any visitor who understands those three understands your estate better than most vendors understand their own, which is the quiet standard this whole cluster has been walking toward since page one.

Does self-hosting help against legal compulsion?

It changes geometry, not physics: data on your hardware subjects to your jurisdiction's rules about your own property, removing the vendor's compliance apparatus (and its foreign subsidiaries) from the chain. For most readers the practical delta is fewer parties with lawful access paths; for high-risk readers the real tools remain encryption at rest with keys in escrow you control and threat modeling done with professionals -- self-hosting is one layer in that stack, never the stack.

Is a home server more or less secure than cloud for a non-expert?

Less, initially: cloud providers field security teams you cannot afford; your first year self-hosting carries learning-curve exposure. More, after the checklist matures: small surface, no shared tenancy, egress control, and drills compound into a posture most consumer accounts never reach. The crossover sits around the maintenance-window habit per the worth-it analysis -- expertise is not the variable; calendared attention is.

What about privacy for the people who contact me?

Their data inherits your posture: correspondents' mail lands on your disk under your retention policy, which is a responsibility as much as a benefit -- publish a one-line privacy note (what you keep, how long, how deleted), honor deletion requests promptly, and encrypt exports. Sovereignty that externalizes its privacy costs onto correspondents is just vendor behavior with better branding, and the community reviews in this cluster read that way too.

Stacking economics: three boxes, not twelve

Running twelve projects on twelve boxes is a space heater; the art is bin-packing by profile: Box A (quiet tier): DNS, VPN, mesh, automation -- 6-8 W, 8 GB, fanless if possible, UPS-mandatory (it is the estate's nervous system). Box B (data tier): backup target, photos, media, git -- disks and RAM here, 16 GB, tolerate fan noise in a closet. Box C (compute tier): CI, inference, monitoring -- bursty loads, 32 GB, schedulable overnight. Measured combined idle: 31 W; combined replacement value in subscriptions: four figures annually, per the cost sheets in the exit guide. The tiering also isolates failure domains: Box C may die mid-batch without touching photos or the doorbell, which is exactly the segmentation the exposure guide preaches at network layer, repeated at hardware layer.

Buying and commissioning notes

Used office mini PCs (1L corporate boxes, ex-lease) deliver the best watt-per-euro in this entire hobby: 8th-12th gen cores, ECC-less but reliable, NVMe slots, and 10 W idles after undervolting folklore is skipped entirely (they ship conservative). Commissioning follows the checklist rows: fresh install from your config repo (NixOS or Debian per the comparison), mesh address and DNS name assigned before services, monitoring agent first so the box is observable before it is useful, and a burn-in week running memtest plus disk scrub cycles before any real data lands. The burn-in week is the project equivalent of the federation's probation period: hardware lies early and honestly if you give it a microphone, and a fan or DIMM that will fail in month three usually confesses in day four.

Noise, heat, and the furniture problem

The three killers of mini-PC deployments are not software: enclosed media cabinets (thermal throttling per the mesh-on-minis Q&A's pilot lesson), bedroom-adjacent fan noise (choose fanless for the quiet tier; measure dB at one meter before arguing with family), and the cable tangle that makes maintenance scary (label both ends, service loop per box, photograph before closing any panel). Households that treat placement as architecture report higher maintenance-window adherence -- the box you can reach and hear is the box you actually maintain, and maintenance, not hardware, is what every uptime story in this cluster finally reduces to.

One procurement footnote that saves real money: buy two of whichever box becomes your data tier, commissioning the second as a cold spare rather than a second server -- the spare sleeps in the escrow shelf with your config already evaluated against it during one annual drill, turning hardware death from a migration event into a swap-and-boot afternoon. The spare costs less than one month of the subscriptions the stack replaces, and its existence converts every other risk row in this list from threat into procedure, which is the psychological dividend runbooks quietly depend on and hardware people chronically underestimate. Label the spare, date its last drill, and keep its firmware matched to the primary -- a spare that diverges is a surprise with a dust cover, and surprises are precisely what the spare existed to eliminate.

What is the realistic all-in cost for the three-box stack?

Used hardware 3× €90-150, RAM and NVMe top-ups €120, UPS €90, switch and cabling €60: roughly €600-750 capital, plus ~€40/year power at regional tariffs. Against the subscription sheet it replaces (photo, password, media, CI, monitoring SaaS: €300-600/year for households and small teams), payback lands in year two -- and year two is when the drills and habits make the estate something subscriptions never were: yours, verifiably.

Can one box run the whole list for a starter household?

Yes at 16 GB with the quiet and data tiers merged, accepting that a CI burst will slow photo sync briefly -- fine for two people, annoying at five. The three-box split is a growth path, not an entry fee: start with Box A plus one merged box, and let the family's complaints (the honestest capacity planner ever built) tell you when the compute tier earns its own silicon.

title: How Often Should I Test Restic Restores, and How?
description: How often to test restic restores: a risk-based schedule, automated partial-restore checks in CI, and the quarterly full-drill procedure that keeps backups honest.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The risk math behind the cadence

Backups fail in three hidden ways: writes that never landed (misconfigured paths, silent exclusions), repositories that corrupted between checks, and restores that break for reasons the backup never exercised (missing keys, changed hostnames, new encryption defaults). Each class has a detection latency you can shrink only by restoring: restic check verifies repository integrity but not that your data is in it; only a restore answers that. Price it: if your dataset's change rate makes a week of loss painful, weekly partials bound the surprise to seven days of drift; quarterly fulls bound the "restore procedure itself is broken" surprise to one quarter, which matches how often hosts, tools, and humans change enough to break procedures.

Weekly: automated partial restores in CI

The canary directory is the trick that makes partials meaningful: a small tree updated daily with known content, so "the restore worked" includes "the newest bytes are the right bytes". Random paths catch exclusion-config rot (someone added --exclude '*.db' two years ago and nobody remembers why). Both results feed one heartbeat metric; missing heartbeats page you, because a verification job that died silently is indistinguishable from a backup that stopped.

Quarterly: the full-restore drill, rehearsed like a fire drill

Ad-hoc triggers: restore immediately after these events

  • Any change to backup configuration, storage, or network path.
  • Ransomware or intrusion suspicion anywhere on the source host.
  • Repository migration, prune-policy change, or restic major-version upgrade.
  • Hardware replacement on the backup target (disks lie quietly first).

Each trigger gets a partial restore within the hour, not the week: the question "did the change break backups?" has a five-minute answer and a three-month answer, and only one of them is acceptable right after a change. Pair with offsite copies per the cluster's offsite-backup guidance once it ships; a drill that restores from the same box that holds the source proves less than you think during a disk event.

Does restic check replace restore testing?

No -- they answer different questions. restic check (and --read-data) verifies repository structures and pack integrity; a restore verifies that your files, paths, permissions, and retention actually produce usable data on a different host. Run check weekly as cheap insurance and restores as the only real proof; teams that substitute one for the other discover the gap during the incident.

How long should a quarterly drill be allowed to take?

As long as your RTO promises, plus 20% margin -- and if the drill exceeds that, the finding is architectural (faster target, parallel streams, narrower retention) rather than procedural. Logging drill duration every quarter builds the trend line that turns "restores feel slow" into a capacity decision with numbers attached.

Should drills restore to production or scratch space?

Scratch, always, except in a real incident: drills must never mutate production state or compete with production IO. The one exception that earns its risk is an annual "cold start" exercise -- rebuild an entire service on bare hardware from repo plus backups -- because that drill tests the thing partials cannot: whether your runbook can recreate a machine from nothing, which is the actual shape of the worst day.

title: Why Is My WireGuard Handshake Failing Behind Double NAT?
description: Why WireGuard handshakes fail behind double NAT: endpoint fixation, keepalives, CGNAT symmetry and the relay patterns that restore connectivity without open ports.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
What a handshake needs, mechanically

WireGuard is silent until traffic flows: a peer sends a handshake initiation to its configured Endpoint, the other side replies, and a session key is established. Behind ordinary (cone) NAT this works because the outgoing packet opens a pinhole the reply can reuse. Behind symmetric NAT -- most CGNAT, many router defaults -- the pinhole is per-destination, and since both peers initiate toward addresses that are not the other's real socket, the two holes never align. The protocol is fine; the address geometry is impossible. Everything below is a way of giving at least one side a predictable address.

Diagnose in sixty seconds

Two patterns separate cleanly. If the reachable peer sees initiation packets arriving from varying source ports, symmetric NAT is rewriting them -- geometry problem, keepalive alone will not fix it. If it sees nothing at all, check the simpler culprits first: firewall rules on the WAN router, wrong Endpoint port, ISP blocking UDP 51820 (rare but real), or clock skew beyond WireGuard's timestamp tolerance, which produces the distinctive "handshake replied but never established" log rhythm.

The three fixes, cheapest first

  1. Keepalives plus one reachable anchor. If at least one peer has a stable address (VPS, IPv6, port-forwarded home), set PersistentKeepalive = 25 on the trapped peers toward it; the warm pinhole lets the anchor relay introductions or simply serve as hub. Cheapest, fixes most homes.
  2. Relay through the hub. Route trapped-to-trapped traffic via the anchor by giving the hub AllowedIPs = 10.66.0.0/24 and enabling forwarding -- the hybrid topology in the mesh tutorial, where this case is exactly why the hub exists.
  3. Change the geometry. IPv6 end-to-end (many CGNATs are IPv4-only), a $3 VPS as one peer's home, or a router that supports full-cone mode. Most durable, most effort; do it for nodes that matter at 3 a.m.

After any fix, verify with wg show handshakes advancing every few minutes and bidirectional transfer counters; then add a monitoring alert on handshake age per peer, because NAT behavior drifts with router firmware updates and ISP reconfigurations -- the mesh that worked in March can exile a node in April without anyone touching a config, and the kerala-mesh pilot learned that lesson one firmware-update Tuesday.

Preventing the class, not the instance

Record each peer's NAT class in your topology file at commissioning time (test with a STUN utility once; symmetric vs cone is stable per router config). Generate keepalive and relay settings from that record instead of troubleshooting per node, and re-run the classification in your quarterly maintenance window alongside the restore drills the cluster preaches elsewhere. Field truth from flood-prone deployments: power-cycle tests double as NAT tests, because routers that reboot into different defaults are how symmetric NAT arrives unannounced.

Does PersistentKeepalone fix double NAT by itself?

No. Keepalives keep a pinhole warm toward the configured Endpoint; when both ends are behind symmetric NAT, each keepalive warms a hole the other side's packets still cannot use, because source ports differ per destination. Keepalives fix cone-NAT roaming and idle-timeout cases; double NAT needs an anchor, a relay, or a geometry change as listed above.

Can two CGNAT peers connect over IPv4 at all?

Only with help: a relay node with a public address (the hub pattern), or hole-punching coordination protocols that WireGuard deliberately does not implement. Accept the relay: one extra hop through your own VPS preserves the mesh's security properties while restoring reachability, and the latency cost for home traffic is milliseconds nobody feels.

Is UDP blocking by the ISP a real possibility?

Occasionally, especially on mobile-carrier CGNAT and some satellite links that shape or drop long UDP flows. Test by moving the WireGuard port to 443/UDP or tunneling over TCP as a diagnostic only; if that "fixes" it, you have your answer and a decision to make -- permanent TCP tunneling costs performance, so most operators switch that peer to a relay path instead.

title: How Can I Host a Website Without a Static IP?
description: How to host a website without a static IP: dynamic DNS, Cloudflare Tunnel and Tailscale Funnel compared, with TLS, caching and the DNS caveats of each route.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The three routes, compared honestly

RouteOpen portsCGNAT-safeControlCostBiggest caveat
Dynamic DNS80/443 at homeNoFull$0Router becomes internet-facing; ISP may block 80/443
Cloudflare TunnelNoneYesEdge policy only$0Traffic decrypts at their edge; vendor in your path
Tailscale FunnelNoneYesYours + DERP relay$0-6Requires Tailscale identity plane
VPS reverse proxyOne, on VPSYesFull$3-6/moYou operate the front door

Cloudflare Tunnel in twelve commands' spirit

Three hardening notes the quickstarts omit. Bind the origin service to 127.0.0.1 so the tunnel is the only path in (otherwise you have quietly re-opened the port you avoided). End the ingress list with an explicit 404 rule -- cloudflared's implicit default is fine until someone edits the file at 1 a.m. And put the tunnel itself under the monitoring heartbeat from your substrate month: a dead cloudflared process presents as "site down" with every local health check green, which is the most confusing ten minutes in self-hosting.

TLS and caching caveats per route

Tunnels terminate TLS at the edge by default; if your threat model wants end-to-end encryption, run TLS to your origin as well (self-signed is fine inside the tunnel, since the tunnel authenticates the origin by service address) or use Tailscale Funnel, where your node's WireGuard-grade identity covers the leg. Caching follows the same split: edge caches give you global speed but also cache your mistakes -- set explicit Cache-Control on immutable assets and keep HTML short-lived or bypassed, or you will debug a stale deploy for an hour. With the VPS route, all of this is your configuration: DNS-01 wildcards, your caddy or nginx edge, and the mesh as the return path, exactly the shape Decentralized.Host nodes run in production.

When buying a static IP is the right answer

Three situations justify the business-line upgrade or the VPS: you run services that cannot tolerate an intermediary (matrix federation with strict TLS pinning, some VoIP), your audience is local and latency through a far-away edge hurts, or compliance requires you to name your egress addresses. Outside those, the tunnel-or-proxy decision stands -- and note that "static IP" bought at home still leaves your router internet-facing, so it solves addressing, not exposure; the exposure question is answered by the same gates and proxies either way, as the exit-the-cloud guide frames it: own the path you can defend, rent the one you can monitor.

Does a tunnel hurt SEO or cause duplicate-content issues?

No, when the public hostname is canonical: search crawlers see one domain with normal HTTPS, and the tunnel is invisible at the HTTP layer. Problems appear only if you expose the same content on multiple public names (tunnel host plus a DDNS host) -- pick one canonical hostname, 301 the rest, and keep certificates valid; crawlers penalize confusion, not topology.

Can I run the tunnel on the same box as the website?

Yes, and it is the common setup: one systemd service for the site, one for cloudflared, origin on localhost. Isolate them anyway -- separate users, and if possible separate containers -- because a vulnerability in either then compromises one role, not both; the federation's node agent follows the same one-role-per-process rule for exactly this reason.

What breaks first when my ISP changes something?

With tunnels: nothing addressing-related, which is their beauty -- but ISP-level MTU or UDP shaping can degrade the tunnel's own outbound link, presenting as slow-large-page complaints. With DDNS: everything, starting with the client cache TTL you forgot to lower. Monitor tunnel latency percentiles alongside site checks so "ISP changed" shows up as a transport graph, not a mystery.

The recurring error in homelab sizing is adding idle numbers and wondering why the box swaps during a photo-sync night: load concurrency, not idle footprint, sets the requirement, and family workloads are bursty by nature -- everyone comes home at six.

The ZFS ARC: the headroom people forget

Containers: the slow leak class

Decide with free monitoring, then stop upgrading

Upgrade only when /proc/pressure/memory shows sustained some-avg10 above ~10 during normal evenings, or swap-in counters move without a backup job running. Below that, more RAM buys silence, not speed -- and silence is what monitoring already gives you. The money usually works harder in the exit guide's other lines: disks with scrub histories, a UPS that has actually been load-tested, or the hour of automation that removes a weekly chore. For what these numbers look like on watt-frugal hardware, the mini-PC project list in this cluster ships measured idle draws per build once it goes live; until then, the mesh pilot's node spec (8 GB, 25 W, three-jurisdiction quorum member) is a datapoint I trust more than any benchmark table.

Is ECC RAM worth it for a home server?

For ZFS pools holding irreplaceable data: yes, cheaply -- used ECC DIMMs cost little and remove an entire class of silent corruption that scrubs can detect but not always repair. For a stateless service box: marginal. The honest rule: ECC matters most where the data cannot be re-fetched, which is exactly the photos-and-documents tier most homelabs underestimate.

Can I run ZFS on 4 GB of RAM?
Does swapping ruin a home server or save it?

A small zram or low-swappiness disk swap saves it: bursts absorb without OOM-killing the wrong process, and PSI tells you when reliance becomes chronic. The failure mode to avoid is default desktop swappiness on a box running databases -- tune vm.swappiness down (10), keep swap as shock absorber, and alert on swap-in rate rather than swap existence; presence is policy, usage is signal.
