title: AI Agent Security Best Practices: Capabilities, Journals, Proofs
description: AI agent security best practices: capability gates, deny-by-default networks, append-only audit journals, signed receipts and the review loop that keeps gates honest.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The threat model in one diagram of words

An agent is a program whose control flow is partly written by untrusted text: user prompts, fetched web pages, tool outputs, and file contents all become instructions to a stochastic interpreter. The attack surface is therefore every byte the agent reads, and the primitive is injection -- text that says "now delete/ exfiltrate/ ignore previous". Consequences scale with capability: a chatbot with no tools can only say harmful things; an agent with shell, filesystem, and network can do harmful things at machine speed with your credentials. The capability-gates paper formalizes exactly this inversion: traditional security assumes the principal knows what it is doing; agent security must assume the principal can be rewritten mid-session by whatever it reads next.

Gates: deny by default, most-specific wins

The grammar's power is testability: 214 recorded agent-behavior cases run against every policy change in CI, so "the gate holds" is a checked property rather than a hope -- the suite and grammar are public in agent-policy-kit and specified normatively in APG-1. Operational rules that keep gates honest: policies live in Git with review like code; denials return typed reasons the agent can plan around (and attackers learn nothing from); and a deny-rate dashboard alerts on spikes, because sudden deny storms mean either an injection campaign or a policy regression, and both deserve a human within the hour.

Sandboxed executors: ceilings as architecture

When a gate grants execution, the executor enforces physics: child processes with memory and CPU ceilings, per-session tmpdirs deleted on close, egress-deny by default with per-tool exceptions, and outputs returned as data never as executable content. The MCP server guide's executor principles generalize beyond MCP: any tool the agent calls should run inside ceilings the agent cannot raise, because "the model promised it was safe" is not a control. Defense in depth here is not paranoia but arithmetic: gates fail at policy rate (text tricks), sandboxes fail at physics rate (cgroups, namespaces), and the intersection of two independent failure probabilities is the number your risk register should carry.

Journals: append-only, hashed, reviewed

Every decision -- grant, deny, needs-approval -- lands in an append-only journal with timestamp, session, tool, capability, verdict, latency, and prompt-hash. Three uses compound: incident review becomes a query rather than an excavation; policy tuning gains deny-rate and grant-pattern telemetry that no benchmark substitutes; and proof-carrying extensions (hashing journal segments, signing them, eventually attaching STARK receipts of gate evaluation per the research agenda) turn "the gate was applied" from assertion into verifiable claim. Retention follows data-protection logic: metadata long, prompt bodies short or never, scrubbing pipelines documented -- the journal proves behavior without becoming the leak it exists to police.

Staged rollouts and the human gate

New tools and policy widenings enter through observation: first week logs-only (the gate would-deny but reports instead of blocking), second week blocked-with-approval (a human answers needs_approval promptly, and promptness is measured because slow approvals train users to route around gates), third week autonomous within scope. Each stage exits on metrics -- would-deny patterns understood, approval latency under SLA, zero unexplained grants. The process sounds bureaucratic until you watch it catch the classic: a tool whose schema allowed path traversal that nobody noticed because the model never tried; observation weeks exist precisely because models explore less than attackers do, and your rollout should assume the difference is temporary.

Beyond the walls: supply chain and model provenance

Agent security ends where your supply chain begins: MCP servers and tool packages are dependencies with executive power, so admit them like contributors -- pinned hashes, reviewed code, minimal scopes, egress-deny at runtime regardless of vendor reputation. Model artifacts get the same treatment (hash-pinned weights per the privacy piece's practice), because a swapped model is a swapped principal. The unified rule across all layers: every component with executive power carries identity (hash), scope (policy), and record (journal). Systems that enforce the triad survive the inevitable injection that lands; systems that skip one layer discover which one they skipped during the incident, which is the most expensive possible way to learn an architecture lesson.

Do guardrail models or classifiers replace gates?

They complement, never replace: classifiers detect injection attempts with useful but imperfect accuracy, while gates enforce capability boundaries deterministically. Use classifiers to raise approval thresholds on suspicious sessions (adaptive friction), and gates to make the worst case bounded regardless of classifier verdicts. A classifier-only design bets the estate on a model's mood; a gate-only design misses context -- together they price risk where it belongs.

How do I secure agents that must browse the web?

Treat fetched content as hostile input by construction: render-free fetchers (text extraction only), egress scoped to allowlisted domains where possible, and zero write-capabilities in the same session as unbounded browsing -- the classic exfiltration channel is a read-capable agent that also holds write or network grants. Split sessions: a reader session summarizes untrusted pages into a sanitized brief; a writer session acts on the brief with gates. Two principals, one workflow, no single session holding both halves of the exfiltration primitive.

What is the first gate to add to an existing ungated agent?

Network egress deny plus filesystem read-only, granted upward per demonstrated need -- it collapses the exfiltration and destruction classes immediately while leaving most legitimate workflows merely inconvenienced (approvals for the exceptions). Measure the approval queue for a week: it is both your usability budget and your attack-log sample, and it hands you the empirical basis for every subsequent grant, which is how policies grow from evidence instead of anxiety.

title: AI Agent Tool-Calling Safety: Gates That Survive Clever Prompts
description: AI agent tool-calling safety: schema constraints, input size negotiation, approval gates, sandboxed executors and the prompt-injection tests your gates must pass.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Schemas as contracts, not suggestions

Capability gates in front of every call

The ordering encodes lessons: capability before scope (a session without the capability never reaches argument parsing), journal before execution (a crash mid-call leaves a record of intent, which forensics needs and apologies cannot supply), and approval as a first-class verdict rather than an exception path bolted on. This is the APG-1 philosophy from the agent security guide applied per tool; the tool-onboarding Q&A covers how tools earn their place in the capability taxonomy in the first place.

Classifying side effects: the write taxonomy

  • Pure reads: cacheable, rate-limited lightly, outputs still untrusted.
  • Local writes: session-scoped paths by default; shared paths require scope tier plus approval.
  • External writes (email, payment, public posts): approval-gated by default with per-session budgets; the "agent emailed the customer" class of incident is entirely this row misfiled as a local write.
  • Irreversible acts (deletes, transfers, publishes): two-person rule or time-delayed execution where stakes warrant; deletion via move-to-trash primitives so undo exists by construction, per the deletion-prevention Q&A.

File the taxonomy in the tool registry beside each schema, and let the gate read it rather than re-dering per call: classification as data, not as code branches, is what keeps the system auditable as tools multiply -- forty tools with per-tool if-statements is forty ways to misfile; forty registry rows with four classes is a reviewable table.

Tool outputs are untrusted input, again

Review loops: where the taxonomy stays honest

Weekly: denial-code histogram (spikes mean schema confusion or capability gaps), approval-hold queue review (holds aging past SLA indicate taxonomy drift, not user patience), and journal sampling of write-class calls reading the planner's stated reason beside the gate's classification -- the sample catches misfiled tools before incidents do. Quarterly: tool sunset review, where unused tools lose capabilities by default and re-earn them on demand; capability sprawl is entropy, and entropy's only opponent is scheduled pruning, the same argument the config-repo orphan reviews make across this entire portfolio. The safety story that survives contact is not a wall of controls but a loop of measurements around five controls, reviewed by named humans on calendars -- everything else is prose.

Should agents be allowed to write their own tools?

Only into a sandboxed executor class with its own gate tier, resource ceilings, and egress-deny, and only with generated-code review before promotion to registered tools -- the promotion path is a human approval by design. Agent-authored tools that skip promotion live and die inside the session sandbox; the boundary between "session scratch" and "registered capability" is the load-bearing wall, and walls need doors with locks, not suggestions.

How do I handle tools that are reads with hidden writes?

Reclassify them: caching layers that persist, analytics calls that phone home, "get" endpoints with rate-state side effects -- audit by running them under strace/network watch at onboarding and file by observed behavior, not by documentation. Tools whose hidden writes cannot be removed get wrapper implementations that make the writes explicit and gated; a wrapper that names the side effect converts a trap into a line item, which is the entire job of this discipline.

Is human approval fatigue a real risk?

Yes, and it is the taxonomy's feedback signal: approval queues with >90% rubber-stamp rates mean the class is over-gated (move down a tier with logging) or under-specified (split the class). Measure stamp-rates per class monthly; the goal is approvals that humans read because they occasionally refuse, and classes where refusal never happens are classes whose gate should be a budget instead -- fatigue is not a human failure, it is a taxonomy error wearing human clothing.

title: Local RAG Pipeline Setup: Chunking, Indexes, and Honest Evaluation
description: A local RAG pipeline setup: chunking strategy, embedding choices, index sizing, retrieval evaluation with real queries and the failure modes that fake good scores.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The pipeline, component by component

  • Ingest: format extractors (markdown, PDF with layout-aware tools, code via tree-sitter splits), normalized to text plus metadata (source path, mtime, owner).
  • Chunk: 300-700 token windows with 10-15% overlap for prose; structural splits for code and docs (functions, sections) beat fixed windows wherever structure exists.
  • Embed: a local embedding model sized to your hardware (the 300M-1B class runs on CPU at ingest-time patience); embeddings versioned per model so re-embedding is a scheduled job, not a surprise.
  • Index: HNSW in-process for small corpora (under ~1M chunks), Qdrant/Weaviate-class when filters and multi-tenancy arrive -- the comparison lives in the cluster's vector-db shelf.
  • Retrieve: dense top-k (k=6-10) merged with BM25 keyword results (reciprocal-rank fusion), metadata filters first (project, date, access tier).
  • Generate: context assembled with chunk ids inline; prompt requires citations by id and forbids answers beyond retrieved content for fact-mode queries.

Quality: the eval loop that precedes tuning

Build a 50-100 query eval set from real questions (support tickets you wished auto-answered, your own search history), each with gold chunk ids and a one-line gold answer. Metrics per configuration change: retrieval recall@k (did gold chunks surface), citation precision (did the model cite what it used), and groundedness (judge-model score plus human spot-checks on twenty). Tune in order of leverage: chunking shape first (recall moves most), then fusion weights, then k, then prompt wording last -- the reverse order is how teams spend weeks polishing prompts over broken retrieval, the RAG equivalent of benchmarking the wrong workload per the benchmark discipline.

Citations: the trust architecture

Operations: ingest as a service, not a script

Continuous ingest watches sources (filesystem events plus nightly full sweeps), dedupes by content hash, and re-embeds only changed chunks; a quarantine queue holds extraction failures and oversize documents for human triage rather than dropping them silently. Access tiers travel in metadata and the retriever filters by session capability before similarity -- retrieval-time authorization is the only place it composes correctly with ranking, because post-retrieval filtering re-ranks nothing and leaks existence information into k. Monitor four numbers: ingest lag, quarantine depth, retrieval recall on the eval set (regression alerts), and citation-drift flags; the agent journaling Q&A's philosophy applies unchanged -- pipelines without heartbeats fail quietly, and quietly is how trust dies.

Honest limits, stated upfront

Start smaller than feels serious: twenty documents, fifty queries, one box. The pipeline's architecture does not change at a hundredfold scale -- chunking discipline, eval loop, citations, authorization-at-retrieval all survive contact with growth -- which is precisely why starting small costs nothing but pride and teaches everything but vendor lock-in -- and twenty documents later, the fifty-query eval set still governs every decision, exactly as designed.

How large can the corpus stay on one box?

Embeddings dominate memory: 1M chunks at 768-dim float32 is ~3 GB plus HNSW graph overhead (~1.5x), comfortably inside 16 GB boxes with quantized indexes (int8) halving it. Ingest time is the real scaling wall (embedding throughput on CPU), so schedule full re-embeds as overnight jobs and keep incremental paths fast -- capacity planning for RAG is capacity planning for a batch ETL that happens to serve search.

Does reranking pay for its latency?
When should I skip RAG and fine-tune instead?

When the knowledge is stable, style/format is the goal, and citation is unnecessary -- fine-tuning shapes behavior, not facts. When answers must track changing documents or carry provenance, RAG wins by construction. Hybrid (tuned style plus retrieved facts) is the mature answer for support bots; the decision rule is provenance: if users must be able to ask "where did this come from", retrieval is not optional, and no amount of tuning manufactures citations it never saw.

title: Self-Hosted Vector Database Comparison: Qdrant vs Chroma vs pgvector
description: Self-hosted vector database comparison: Qdrant vs Chroma vs pgvector on recall, memory, ops burden and backup story — with the small-dataset verdict teams need.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Recall first: the number that is not a differentiator

The three operational stories

  • Chroma: embedded or client-server; the embedded mode is prototyping gold (vectors in your process, zero services) and the trap: moving to server mode later changes consistency and persistence semantics you assumed. Use it to prove retrieval value in a weekend, graduate deliberately.
  • pgvector: vectors as a column beside your relational rows; HNSW indexes in recent versions make million-row workloads practical; joins and filters are plain SQL, which your team already reviews competently. Ceiling: very large corpora and high QPS push you out, but "very large" is farther than most estates ever walk.

Memory and persistence behavior under stress

The stress tests that decide long-term happiness: kill -9 during indexing (Qdrant's WAL replays cleanly; embedded Chroma's durability depends on your embedding discipline; pgvector inherits Postgres crash recovery -- the strongest story of the three, because it is Postgres's story). RAM exhaustion (Qdrant's quantization and on-disk modes degrade gracefully; pgvector shares the database's memory pool, so budget shared_buffers with vectors inside the same envelope per the RAM sizing guide; embedded Chroma competes with your application for the same heap). Backup integration (pgvector dumps with the database -- one tool, one drill; Qdrant snapshots need their own row in the backup chain; embedded stores hide inside app directories until someone audits them, which is how they get missed by restic include-lists, the silent-exclusion class from the restic guide).

Choosing in one paragraph, with the graduation path

Prototype in Chroma embedded because weekends are short; if retrieval earns production space, choose by data gravity: vectors beside relational truth that must transact together go to pgvector (one backup, one drill, one story); vectors as their own corpus with heavy filtering and quantization needs go to Qdrant (one service, one snapshot hook). Both graduations keep the retrieval layer behind your gateway's interface so the engine swap is a config commit, not a client migration -- the alias-table trick from the gateway guide applied to search. And whichever you run, pin embedding model versions in the same manifest as the index: embeddings are the schema of vector land, and an unversioned embedding model is a schema migration nobody scheduled, discovered by recall drift that no dashboard can attribute.

Do I need reranking with any of these?
How large before leaving a single box?

Single-box comfortable ceiling: ~5M int8-quantized 768-dim vectors with HNSW in 32 GB RAM including headroom, at interactive latencies. Beyond that, shard by tenant or time (both engines support it) before buying clustering complexity -- sharding on a dimension you already filter by is free partitioning, and free partitioning beats purchased orchestration every time the filter exists.

Is disk-based (on-disk HNSW) worth it?

For cold corpora queried occasionally (archives, compliance search), emphatically yes: NVMe-backed indexes cut RAM 5-10x at 2-4x latency, a trade archives happily make. For interactive RAG, keep hot collections resident and archive cold ones to on-disk or to restic shelves with a rehydrate runbook -- tiering vectors like tiering storage is the same discipline at a new altitude, and the runbook row is what makes the cold tier honest.

Whichever engine you choose, commission it with the four artifacts every other service in this cluster receives: a runbook page (reindex procedure, restore-from-snapshot steps, embedding-version migration), a heartbeat in monitoring (index lag, query p95, RAM headroom), a backup row naming exactly what is backed up (snapshots or dumps plus the embedding manifest -- backing up vectors without their embedding pin is backing up ciphertext without its key), and a sunset review date for the day corpus growth crosses the single-box ceiling. Engines differ in features; estates differ in whether those four rows exist, and it is the rows, not the engine, that decide whether year two of your retrieval stack reads as operations or as archaeology. Pin the embedding model hash in the same manifest as the index, journal every reindex with its before/after recall on the eval set, and let the manifest plus journal answer the only two questions an audit will ever ask about your retrieval stack: which vectors are these, and what changed them last.

When the sunset date arrives and the corpus has outgrown the box, graduation is a config commit plus a reindex window, not a rescue: engines behind one interface, embeddings pinned, backups drilled -- the three properties that turn any future migration into an event with a schedule instead of an incident with a story. Schedules, unlike stories, can be slept through; and a retrieval stack that can migrate in its sleep is the retrieval stack its owners recommend to friends, which is the only endorsement this cluster has ever accepted as evidence.

title: LLM Inference on CPU Hardware: What Actually Runs, How Fast
description: LLM inference on CPU hardware: what runs at usable speeds, token rates by core count and quantization, and the workloads where CPU-only is the right call.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The bandwidth arithmetic that decides everything

Box (bandwidth)3B Q87B Q413B Q4
8-core DDR4 (~35 GB/s)9.2 tok/s7.1 tok/s2.2 tok/s
8-core DDR5 (~60 GB/s)15.8 tok/s11.9 tok/s4.1 tok/s
M2 16 GB (~100 GB/s)26 tok/s19 tok/s7 tok/s

Where CPU inference actually fits

  • Personal assistants and drafting: 7-12 tok/s reads faster than most people edit; the 8 GB RAM Q&A covers the memory envelope.
  • Gate and classification heads: small models scoring agent actions or routing queries -- milligram workloads where CPU keeps the GPU free for serving.
  • Air-gapped and regulated corners: boxes that may never contain a GPU (policy, power, supply) still deserve assistants; CPU inference is the sovereignty floor of the stack.

Tuning levers, in order of payoff

Threads at physical-core count (hyperthread oversubscription hurts bandwidth-bound loops more than compute-bound ones); flash attention on; KV cache quantized at q8 for contexts over 4k (memory bandwidth is the budget, cache is a spender); prompt processing chunked so first-token latency stays interactive while batch prefetch warms; and model choice by bandwidth division, not by parameter vanity -- a 3B Q8 often beats a 7B Q4 on both quality-per-byte and tokens-per-second for narrow tasks, a trade the quantization comparison prices per task family. Measure after each lever with a fixed 200-token generation harness; CPU inference tuning without a harness is weather forecasting with a wet finger.

The honest ceiling, and the GPU handshake

Three workloads should leave CPU immediately: multi-user interactive serving (concurrency divides your already-modest bandwidth), long-context generation beyond 16k (KV traffic joins weight traffic in the same narrow pipe), and frontier-quality demands (the models that satisfy them do not fit the bandwidth budget at any quantization that preserves them). The mature architecture therefore treats CPU and GPU as one fleet: CPU boxes absorb batch, embed, and gate workloads plus overflow drafting; GPU boxes hold interactive sessions; the gateway routes by model class and quota. That handshake -- cheap silicon doing what cheap silicon is good at, expensive silicon rationed to what only it can do -- is the same shape as the federation's node classes in decentralized.hosting, because capacity economics does not care whether the resource is watts, watts, or watts.

Does AVX-512 or AMX change the picture?

Meaningfully on supported silicon: AVX-512 adds 20-40% on quantized kernels, AMX-class matmul units more on INT8 paths -- check your CPU flags and your runtime build (llama.cpp prints the enabled ISA set at startup; if it says AVX2 on an AVX-512 box, you left a third of your machine in the box). The bandwidth rule still caps the ceiling; SIMD changes the constant, not the law.

Can multiple CPU users share one box efficiently?
Is CPU inference worth it versus a $200 used GPU?

Usually yes for the first step: CPU needs no drivers, no VRAM envelope, no power draw beyond the box you own, and fails boringly. The used GPU upgrades tokens-per-watt dramatically but adds the VRAM mathematics, thermals, and driver maintenance from the VRAM guide. Sequence: prove the workload on CPU, measure its value, then let the measurement buy the GPU -- purchases after measurements age better than purchases before them, in inference as in every other line of the cost sheet.

When someone asks why the household keeps a box that "only" manages seven tokens a second, point at that chart and at the invoice it replaced: seven tokens a second, multiplied by every night of the year, is a private library of summaries, embeddings, and drafts that never left the building -- and speed was never the property anyone was actually buying. The property was custody, and custody, measured in watts and journal lines, is the one benchmark no vendor chart can quote back at you.

Read the labor line twice: it is where self-hosting loses small deployments and wins disciplined ones. The automated stack from this cluster (gateway quotas, journaling, heartbeat monitoring, IaC rebuilds) holds ops near two hours weekly; unautomated stacks double it and invert the comparison at every volume -- automation is not a virtue here, it is the cost structure, exactly as the exit guide's labor analysis found for general infrastructure.

Break-even math you can redo in a spreadsheet

The unpriced columns, named anyway

  • Privacy and data gravity: prompts never leaving your estate has compliance and IP value no list price captures; the privacy piece sizes what leaves by default.
  • Pricing immunity: vendor price and model-deprecation shocks become news, not decisions; budget planning loses a volatility column.
  • Model freedom: fine-tunes, quantization experiments, and mixture routing per workload -- per-slot model choice is a quality lever cloud tiers rent back to you as plan upgrades.
  • Latency locality: on-LAN inference removes WAN round-trips from interactive loops; at drafting cadences, 40 ms saved per token stream is felt, not measured.

The hybrid answer most estates actually land on

For readers building their first sheet, three shortcuts keep it honest: price cloud at the p95 month, not the average (bursts are the bill); value ops labor at your real replacement cost, never zero (zero is the number that makes sheets lie); and amortize hardware over three years with a residual note, then re-run at two and four years as sensitivity rows. Three sensitivity rows convert a verdict into a range, and ranges survive contact with next quarter's pricing email -- which is the entire purpose of the exercise: not to declare a winner forever, but to own the arithmetic well enough that forever is not required, and every renewal conversation starts from your ledger instead of their brochure. Keep every yearly sheet in the config repository beside the gateway configs, dated and signed by whoever ran the numbers; a cost history you own is the only inflation index that applies to your actual workload, and it compounds in credibility exactly as the proofs compound in trust.

Does the sheet change for fine-tuned models?

Decisively: cloud fine-tune hosting prices per deployed model-hour whether you query it or not, while owned silicon amortizes across every fine-tune you run. Estates with two or more persistent custom models cross break-even at a fraction of the token volumes above, which is why research-adjacent teams often self-host first for tuning and only later for base serving -- follow the fixed-cost lines, they point the way.

How do I cost GPU depreciation honestly?
What volume should trigger the first GPU purchase?

When CPU-only latency stops serving your interactive slots (per the CPU piece's concurrency physics) or when monthly cloud spend exceeds the used-GPU price divided by 24 -- whichever arrives first. Both are gateway-log queries, not forecasts: buy after the measurement shows the shape of your traffic, and let the journal entry that justified the purchase become the first line of the asset's design note.

title: How Much VRAM Do I Need for a 7B Model at Q4, Q8, and FP16?
description: Exact VRAM math for 7B models at Q4, Q8 and FP16 including KV-cache headroom, plus the settings that fit a 7B model into 6 GB and 8 GB cards.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The three-term arithmetic

VRAM demand is the sum of three terms. Weights: parameters x bytes-per-weight (FP16 = 2, Q8 = 1, Q4 = 0.5, plus roughly 3-5% overhead for quantization scales). KV cache: 2 x layers x kv-heads x head-dim x context x bytes-per-element, doubled because key and value are separate tensors. Overhead: CUDA/graph arenas, allocator fragmentation, and the runtime's own footprint -- budget 0.5-1.5 GB and treat anything less as luck. For a Llama-shaped 7B (32 layers, 32 kv-heads pre-GQA, head-dim 128) at FP16 with 4k context, the KV term alone is about 2 GB; with GQA (8 kv-heads) it drops to about 0.5 GB, which is why modern 7B models fit 4-bit plus 8k context inside 6 GB cards.

Reference table: 7B across quantizations

PrecisionBytes/weightWeightsKV @ 8k (GQA)Realistic totalFits
FP162.014.0 GB1.0 GB15.5-16.5 GB24 GB card, or 16 GB tight
Q8_01.07.2 GB1.0 GB8.5-9.5 GB12 GB card comfortably
Q4_K_M0.543.9 GB1.0 GB4.8-5.6 GB6 GB card; 8 GB with room
Q4_K_M + 32k ctx0.543.9 GB4.0 GB8.3-9.2 GB8 GB tight, 12 GB safe

Read the last row carefully: context length is the silent budget-killer. KV cache grows linearly with context and with batch size, so a 4-bit model that idles at 5 GB can exceed 9 GB under a long document or a few concurrent users. If you serve rather than chat, cap context and batch explicitly -- the cost model in the ai-infrastructure reference stack treats "VRAM per concurrent session" as a first-class capacity unit for exactly this reason.

Measure, don't estimate: a 60-second check

Every runtime reports actual allocation; trust it over any table, including mine. With llama.cpp server running:

Reproduce the table by varying --ctx-size and quantization; you should see the weights line track bytes-per-weight and the KV line track context linearly. When a community post claims "7B fits in 4 GB", compare their KV line and context to yours before believing the headline -- most such claims are 2k context, batch 1, and no headroom.

Making 7B fit a 6 GB or 8 GB card

  • Choose Q4_K_M or IQ4_XS -- the K-quants keep attention weights sharper than naive 4-bit; quality loss on coding and math benchmarks is typically 1-2%, far less than the loss from dropping to 3-bit.
  • Cap context to what you use (--ctx-size 8192), and enable flash attention so the KV term stays resident-efficient.
  • Offload nothing if it fits: partial GPU offload (some layers on CPU) saves VRAM but can halve throughput; it is a fallback, not a tuning strategy.
  • One model per card: two "small" models sharing 8 GB fragment the allocator and OOM at the worst moment; use a gateway with queueing instead, as in the XFree local-assistant configuration.

The privacy angle deserves one sentence because it drives most of these deployments: a 7B at Q4 on a six-year-old GPU produces genuinely useful assistant, summarization, and classification capacity with zero tokens leaving your building -- the threat-model argument is developed in the cluster index on AI Infrastructure & MCP, and the services page covers assisted setups.

Does quantization change the VRAM math for CPU-only boxes?

The arithmetic is identical, but the scarce resource becomes RAM bandwidth, not capacity: a Q4 7B needs about 5 GB of RAM yet generates tokens at whatever your memory bus allows (typically 4-9 tok/s on DDR4). Capacity questions and speed questions have different answers on CPU -- see the cluster piece on CPU inference when it ships.

Why does my measured VRAM exceed the sum of weights and KV?

Allocator arenas and compute graphs reserve contiguous blocks; CUDA context itself takes 300-500 MB before your model loads. Measure the empty-runtime baseline first (load nothing, read nvidia-smi), then subtract -- the residual is your true overhead term, and it is mostly fixed per process.

Is FP16 ever worth it for a 7B model locally?

For quality-sensitive evaluation runs and as a baseline when benchmarking quantization loss, yes -- that is exactly what it is for. For daily assistant use, Q8 is visually indistinguishable in most tasks at half the VRAM, and Q4_K_M is the pragmatic daily driver; keep FP16 as the ruler, not the tool.

title: Can I Run an LLM on 8GB of RAM (No GPU)?
description: Can you run an LLM on 8 GB of RAM without a GPU? Yes for 3B-7B at Q4: expected token rates, swap traps, context limits and settings that keep it responsive.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
What actually fits, with the arithmetic shown

Model / quantWeightsKV @ 4kSystem+runtimeFits 8 GB?
3B Q8_03.4 GB0.5 GB~2 GBcomfortably
7B Q4_K_M4.1 GB1.0 GB~2 GByes, ~1 GB spare
7B Q5_K_M4.9 GB1.0 GB~2 GBtight; close apps
13B Q4_K_M7.6 GB1.5 GB~2 GBno -- swap death

The system+runtime row is the forgotten term: OS, shell, editor, and the runtime's own arenas consume 1.5-2.5 GB on a lived-in machine before the model loads. Measure your idle baseline (free -h after login, not at boot) and subtract it from 8 GB before believing any model-size chart, including this one -- the table's spare column is what separates "loads" from "loads and stays responsive while your editor is open".

Settings that keep it usable

Thread count surprises people: more threads than physical cores adds synchronization overhead and memory pressure without tokens, so start at physical-core count and tune down if the box feels sticky. KV quantization (-ctk/-ctv q8_0) halves the cache's RAM at quality cost measurable only with calipers at 4k context. --mlock pins weights so the OS cannot page them out under editor pressure -- the single most effective flag for "it was fast yesterday" complaints on shared boxes.

Token-rate expectations, honestly

The swap trap and how to see it coming

When weights plus KV plus lived-in OS exceed RAM, Linux swaps cold pages and generation becomes seek-bound: tokens arrive in bursts separated by disk stalls, fans scream, and the model "feels broken". Detect with /proc/pressure/memory (some-avg10 above ~5 during generation) or vmstat's si/so columns moving at all. Responses, in order: drop context length first (KV shrinks linearly), then quantization tier, then close apps, then -- last -- add swap as a crash absorber rather than a capacity plan. The cluster's slow-LLM diagnosis Q&A walks the same signals from the other direction, and the serving guide shows what changes when this box graduates to a GPU.

Does an M-series Mac change the answer?

Decisively: unified memory means the "8 GB" includes what GPUs would call VRAM, and the memory bandwidth (60-100 GB/s) doubles or triples CPU-class token rates -- 7B Q4 at 10-15 tok/s is ordinary. The tables above describe x86 DDR geometry; on Apple silicon, treat 8 GB as workable and 16 GB as comfortable, with the same context-length discipline applying to KV headroom.

Can I run two small models instead of one 7B?

Rarely worth it at 8 GB: two 3B models consume the same RAM as one 7B while splitting attention and cache, and routing logic adds latency you cannot afford at these rates. The better split is one resident model plus on-demand loads for special tasks (a coder variant swapped in for coding sessions), accepting the 10-20 s load time as the price of variety on small boxes.

title: Why Is My Local LLM Slow, and How Do I Fix It?
description: Why your local LLM is slow and how to fix it: VRAM versus RAM residency, thread counts, KV-cache quantization, context bloat and flags that pinpoint the cause.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Residency: the first number to check

Inference speed is bounded by memory bandwidth times residency fraction: every layer that must page in from disk or host RAM per token multiplies latency. GPU boxes: nvidia-smi shows model bytes versus allocated VRAM -- if weights exceed VRAM, runtimes offload layers to CPU and tokens crawl at DDR speeds while the GPU idles, the signature being high CPU and 5% GPU utilization. CPU boxes: /proc/pressure/memory above ~5 during generation means swap involvement. Fixes in order: smaller quant, shorter context (KV is resident memory too), close competitors, or add the hardware the VRAM math Q&A sizes. Never "fix" residency by raising swap: that converts a slow assistant into a disk-thrashing heater.

Threads: the second number, and the classic overshoot

Context bloat: the slow creep

KV cache grows linearly with context and batch; a "4k default" workflow that became "paste the whole repository" multiplies per-token attention cost and memory pressure simultaneously. Symptoms: first tokens fast, degradation within a session, recovery after /clear. Responses: cap context at what tasks actually use (the histogram signal from the serving guide), quantize KV at q8 where memory binds, and chunk retrieval-style workloads instead of pasting corpora -- a RAG pipeline with 2k retrieved context beats a 16k paste on quality and speed, which is the rare win-win this field offers.

Runtime and hardware mismatch

Thermals: the environmental culprit

Laptops and mini PCs throttle under sustained matmul: clock graphs sagging after 90 seconds while tokens/second sag with them is the signature. Check with sensors or vendor tools during a benchmark run; remedies are physical (airflow, undervolting where supported, a $12 stand) or scheduling (batch jobs at night, interactive use bursty). One measured case from the pilot fleet: a mini PC behind a TV panel lost 38% throughput until relocation -- no config change has ever bought that much, which is why thermals earn the last section and never the last guess.

Why is the first token slow but the rest fast?

Prompt processing (prefill) is compute-bound over the whole context, while generation is bandwidth-bound per token; long prompts therefore front-load seconds of work. Mitigations: prompt caching for repeated prefixes, chunked prefill on vLLM, and not pasting the novel when a paragraph suffices -- prefill cost is the honest price of context, payable once per unique prefix.

Does enabling flash attention change quality?

No: it is an exact algorithmic rearrangement (tiling with online softmax), not an approximation -- identical outputs modulo float associativity noise. It changes memory (KV residency drops) and speed (attention kernels fuse), which is why every serving recipe here turns it on; quantized KV, by contrast, is a real approximation and belongs to the quality conversation instead.

My tokens/s fluctuate wildly between runs. Why?

Usually scheduler noise: background indexing, backup windows, or browser tabs competing for bandwidth and cores. Benchmark with the box quiesced and report medians with spreads; if fluctuation persists on an idle box, suspect thermals or power profiles (laptop on battery caps clocks), both of which show in clock logs during the run -- measure the environment before blaming the model, which is innocent more often than its reputation.

title: Is It Safe to Paste My Code Into an LLM? A Practical Rule Set
description: Is it safe to paste code into an LLM? A practical rule set: secret scrubbing, repo-level policies, local models for sensitive cores and what ToS actually permit.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
What actually happens to pasted code

On submission, your prompt transits TLS to the provider, enters their inference queue, and is processed under their data-processing agreement: enterprise tiers typically contract zero retention and no training use; free and prosumer tiers have historically retained prompts for abuse review with training-use opt-outs buried in settings. Abuse-review pipelines mean humans or classifiers can see flagged content; legal process means courts can compel what retention preserved. None of this is villainy -- it is architecture with policy attached -- but it is their architecture and their policy, and the local-privacy piece exists precisely because some codebases deserve an answer that terminates at your own RAM instead.

The rule set that survives real workdays

  • Scrub automatically. A paste-guard (editor hook or clipboard wrapper) stripping secrets patterns, internal hostnames, and customer identifiers catches the routine leaks before judgment enters; humans are unreliable filters at 4 p.m. on a Friday.
  • Minimize scope. Paste the function and its types, not the file and its imports; questions about logic rarely need surrounding context, and every extra line is extra exposure with zero answer quality.
  • Know your tier. Enterprise contract with zero retention: broad paste latitude. Prosumer subscription: opt out of training explicitly and treat retention as real. Free tier: assume review eyes and act accordingly.
  • Route sensitive cores local. Crypto key handling, unreleased product logic, regulated data: the localhost endpoint from your gateway handles these at Q4 quality that beats no-assistance every time, per the quantization decisions in this cluster.

The gray zones worth naming

Dependency manifests and stack traces are usually fine (public artifacts by nature) but can fingerprint your employer to a motivated reader -- relevant for unreleased work, where even a crash signature reveals feature shapes. Test fixtures are the classic trojan: "harmless sample data" that contains a real customer record three rows down, which is why scrubbers should parse fixtures structurally rather than regex secrets alone. And copied-from-internet code carries license questions orthogonal to privacy: pasting GPL snippets into a proprietary context via an assistant does not launder the license, a conversation your legal team should have before an auditor has it for you.

The local/cloud split that keeps flowing

Writing this down as team policy

A one-page policy beats a training deck: name the tiers and their latitude, list the always-local categories (keys, regulated data, unreleased core logic), mandate the scrubber, and link the routing setup guide so compliance is configuration rather than conscience. Review quarterly alongside dependency and model-pin reviews, because vendor terms drift and so do workflows. The policy's success metric is boring and measurable: zero scrubber catches of real secrets per quarter (training working) and stable local-route share (routing working) -- two numbers in the same dashboard as everything else this cluster monitors, because privacy that is not measured is preference, not posture.

Do "anonymous" code snippets still identify my company?

Frequently, yes: internal naming conventions, bespoke framework shims, and error-string dialects fingerprint organizations the way prose fingerprints authors. If anonymity matters (consulting across competing clients, security research), rewrite identifiers and idioms before pasting, or route local -- the rewrite cost is minutes and the alternative is a disclosure conversation measured in lawyers.

Is using cloud LLMs on open-source code I maintain a problem?

No: the code is public by definition, and assistance on it leaks nothing unpublished. The interesting edge is unpublished fixes to public code (security patches pre-disclosure), which belong in the sensitive category until the disclosure window closes -- coordinated-disclosure timelines and cloud retention windows make uncomfortable bedfellows, and the security.txt culture exists precisely to keep such windows respected.

What about IDE assistants that send repository context automatically?

Treat autocomplete-with-context as continuous pasting: audit what the plugin transmits (many send surrounding files), scope it per repository via config (sensitive repos pointed at the local endpoint), and verify with one network-captured session rather than vendor documentation. The gateway's per-key journals make local routing observable; for cloud plugins, the plugin's own telemetry docs plus a packet capture are your only witnesses -- check them once per plugin upgrade, because defaults drift.

title: How Do I Stop an AI Agent From Deleting Files?
description: How to stop an AI agent deleting files: read-only mounts, path-scoped policies, confirmation gates, snapshot-before-run workflows and journal alerts on deny.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Why behavior tricks fail and capability gates don't

Prompt-level instructions ("never delete files") are suggestions to a stochastic system; prompt injection, ambiguous plans, and plain misjudgment all bypass them routinely. Capability gates are different in kind: the agent's tool call is checked against policy before execution, in code, with deny-by-default semantics. An agent told to "clean up the workspace" against a read-only mount produces a logged deny and an adapted plan -- the failure is absorbed by architecture, not by the model's mood that day. This is the core argument of the APG-1 specification: make the safe path the only path.

The four-layer stack, in order of importance

  1. Read-only by default. The agent's filesystem tool sees a read-only view; writes happen only through an explicit fs_write tool whose policy grants specific path prefixes. Most sessions never need it.
  2. Path-scoped grants. fs:~/proj/src:rw beats "filesystem access" the way least privilege beats root: the blast radius of a bad decision is one directory, and the journal shows every grant exercised.
  3. Confirmation gates for destructive verbs. rm, recursive moves, force-push, schema drops: policy returns needs_approval, a human (or a stricter policy tier) decides, and the decision is journaled with prompt-hash.
  4. Snapshots before runs. A git commit, ZFS snapshot, or restic backup taken automatically at session start converts "deleted" into "reverted in 40 seconds" -- the difference between an anecdote and an incident.

Proving the gates: deletion attempts as test cases

When something still gets deleted

Assume it eventually will -- through a tool you forgot to gate, or a grant scoped one directory too wide. The response plan is what makes that survivable: snapshot-first means restore is routine; the journal means root-cause is a query ("which grant allowed this path?"); and the postmortem ends with a policy diff, not a promise. Teams that treat deletion incidents as policy bugs converge quickly; teams that treat them as model misbehavior keep relitigating the same prompt forever.

Is a confirmation prompt for every write too annoying in practice?

Yes -- which is why confirmations attach to destructive verbs and out-of-scope paths, not to writes generally. Scoped rw grants inside a project feel invisible in daily use; the friction concentrates exactly where the risk does. If users start rubber-stamping approvals, tighten scopes or add an auto-allow tier for file types; never remove the journal.

Does read-only mounting break build tools that need caches?

Often -- so grant caches explicitly as their own prefix (fs_write:~/.cache/build:rw) rather than widening the project grant. Caches are precisely the directory you can afford to lose, which makes them the perfect pressure valve: the agent gets writability where destruction is cheap, and your source tree stays a fortress.

Can the agent delete files via exec instead of fs tools?

Only if exec is granted -- and in the policy above, it is denied except one pinned command. That is the point of evaluating every capability through the same gate: agents do not care which door they use, so neither can you. Audit your tool list quarterly for accidental shells: interpreters, package runners, and editors are all exec in disguise.

title: What Is MCP For, in Plain Terms?
description: What MCP is for in plain terms: a standard plug for tools and context so agents can call your systems safely — with one worked example from schema to sandbox.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The problem it solves, in one diagram of words

Without a standard, three agent frameworks wanting four tools need twelve bespoke integrations, each with its own auth, serialization, error semantics, and security review. With MCP, the same world needs three plus four: every server implements the protocol once, every host speaks it once, and the contract between them is a JSON Schema plus a capability handshake. The integrations stop being projects and become configuration -- which is exactly what happened to printers, storage, and charging before it.

What MCP is not

  • Not a model API. It carries tool calls and data, not tokens; your LLM endpoint stays separate.
  • Not a sandbox. The protocol validates shapes, not consequences -- execution boundaries are still your job (child processes, ceilings, policy gates).

That last distinction matters operationally: a server honestly declaring an exec tool is protocol-correct, and pointing an agent at it without a deny-by-default gate is still an incident waiting for a prompt. The gate layer -- APG-1 style policies, journals, approvals -- sits between negotiation and execution, and it is where the MCP tutorial spends most of its length.

A sixty-second worked example

Notice what is absent: no shell, no file paths, no credentials in arguments. The server's entire surface to the model is a name, a description, and a bounded schema -- which is precisely why the ecosystem can afford to let strangers publish servers while still sleeping at night, provided hosts enforce policy at the gate.

When you should (and shouldn't) reach for it

Use MCP when multiple hosts or agents need the same tools, when you want policy enforcement at a single choke point, or when you are tired of maintaining SDK glue. Skip it for a one-script automation (call the function directly -- indirection is a cost), and skip it when your "tool" is really arbitrary code execution: that is a sandbox product, not a protocol server. For building your first server end to end, the companion guide how to build an MCP server walks the four components; for keeping agents harmless once connected, see stopping agents from deleting files, and the reference implementation with policy gates lives at mcp-prove-server.

Does MCP work with local models, or only cloud APIs?

Entirely with local models: MCP sits between the agent loop and your tools, so the model's location is irrelevant. Local setups actually benefit most, because the gate layer gives you an enforcement point that cloud vendors otherwise provide -- and with local inference plus MCP gates, no part of the loop leaves your machine by default.

Is MCP secure enough to expose to the internet?

The protocol is not the security boundary; your transport auth, tenant isolation, and policy gates are. Stdio servers have no network surface at all. Streamable-HTTP servers must carry real authentication and per-tenant sessions before anything else -- treat an unauthenticated public MCP endpoint as an unauthenticated shell endpoint, because with a permissive server, it is.

How is MCP different from function calling in model APIs?

Function calling is a model-vendor feature for passing structured arguments; MCP is a cross-vendor session protocol with discovery, negotiation, cancellation, and resources. They compose: a host may translate MCP tools into vendor function schemas per model. MCP's added value is portability and the single enforcement choke point -- vendor function calling gives you neither across vendors.

title: How Do I Add Tools to an AI Agent Safely?
description: How to add tools to an AI agent safely: capability reviews, schema minimization, sandboxed executors, staged rollouts and the kill switch you test on day one.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The five stages, with their exit criteria

  • 1 Schema review: parameters bounded and typed, no catch-alls, description states side effects truthfully; exit: reviewer signs the schema diff.
  • 2 Classification: run the tool under strace/network watch with adversarial inputs; file by observed behavior into the four-class taxonomy from the safety guide; exit: registry row with class and evidence link.
  • 3 Sandbox trial: two weeks in a session-scoped capability (path-scoped writes, egress-deny), all calls journaled with planner reasons; exit: transcript sample reviewed, no unclassified side effects observed.
  • 4 Promotion review: invocation histogram (used at all?), denial-code spread (schema confusion?), approval-stamp rate (over-gated?); exit: budgets set per class, approval tier confirmed by stamp-rate rule.
  • 5 Registry life: owner named, sunset date defaulting to six months, re-earn on demand; exit criteria for retirement: zero invocations two quarters.

The onboarding traps, observed in registry audits

Documentation optimism: tools described as reads that persist caches or phone home -- stage 2's strace exists precisely because vendors document intent, not behavior. Scope inflation at promotion: a tool trialed path-scoped arriving at registry with global write "for convenience" -- promotion diffs the capability row against trial capability, and the diff needs a signature. Description drift: schema updated, description stale, planner behavior shifts silently -- descriptions are part of the schema diff, enforced by review template. Orphan ownership: tools whose owner left the team keep capabilities by inertia; sunset dates plus quarterly orphan pruning (the config-repo habit, applied to registries) close the loop, per the pruning philosophy in the safety guide's review section.

Metrics that make promotion a decision, not a mood

Four numbers per trial tool: invocation count by session class (is anyone using it, and who), denial rate by code (schema friction), approval-stamp rate (tier calibration), and journal-sample disagreement rate (planner's stated reason versus gate's classification, sampled twenty calls). Publish them in the promotion review doc beside the schema diff; a tool whose numbers nobody reads gets default sunset at six months, which converts registry entropy into scheduled arithmetic -- the same trick the config orphan reviews use, and for the same reason: entropy's only reliable opponent is a calendar with an owner.

Can stages be compressed for urgent tools?

Stages 1-2 never (schema and classification are the load-bearing walls); stage 3 can compress to 72 hours with doubled journal sampling for internal-curated tools, never for open-web-sourced ones. The compression rule is written in the registry policy so urgency debates happen once, at policy time, rather than per tool at 5 p.m. on a deadline day.

How do wrappers fit the staged path?

Wrappers (implementations that make hidden writes explicit, bound unbounded parameters, or add approval prompts) are stage-2 outputs: the wrapper is the tool, the wrapped binary is its dependency, and the registry row cites both. Reviewing wrappers means reviewing the delta they add -- usually under two hundred lines -- which is why wrapper-first onboarding is often faster than arguing with an upstream tool's actual behavior.

What kills a tool fastest post-promotion?

Keep one paragraph per tool beside its registry row -- a biography: why it arrived, what it replaced, what it was expected to change. Biographies make sunset reviews short and re-adoption decisions informed; their absence is felt only during the conversation that needs them most, which is always the one running against an incident timer.

title: Should I Log Every Agent Action? What Goes in the Journal?
description: Should you log every agent action? What belongs in an append-only journal, retention math, privacy scrubbing and how receipts make logs proof-grade.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
Journal schema: seven fields, zero opinions

Hash-and-size args keep the journal readable at scale and privacy-defensible by default; full args stay in a tier-2 store with access logging, opened only under incident review policy. The reason field is the planner's own text captured at decision time -- post-hoc summaries lie, contemporaneous quotes do not, and the gap between reason and outcome is where misbehavior becomes visible: a write justified by "user asked" with no user turn in the session transcript is an injection signature, detectable by joining two logs nobody thought to join.

The three disciplines the journal enables

  • Forensics: session replay as a query (all calls, verdicts, reasons in order); incident timelines assembled in minutes instead of archaeology weeks.
  • Calibration: denial histograms per tool and class, approval-stamp rates, reason-versus-classification disagreement sampling -- the measurement loop from the onboarding Q&A runs entirely off journal aggregates.
  • Trust accounting: monthly per-session summaries (calls by class, writes by scope tier, denials) published to the humans who own the agent; trust that is reported survives, trust that is assumed expires at the first incident.

Journal operations: append-only, shipped, sampled

Append-only with hash-chaining (each entry references the previous hash) makes silent edits detectable -- the integrity trick from the federation manifests, applied to logs; ship to the backup target nightly because local journals die with local disks per the offsite guide; retain hot ninety days, cold per policy with the access log of every cold open. Sample weekly: twenty random write-class entries read by a human comparing reason to outcome -- the sample is cheap, and the knowledge that a sample exists changes how everyone writes reasons, which is the cheapest behavioral control in the entire stack.

Alerts off the journal, not off the agent

Four standing alerts: denial-code two-sigma spikes (schema confusion or capability gap), write-scope tier escalation (a session touching a higher tier than its capability row -- always an incident or a taxonomy bug), reason-absence on write-class calls (planner invoking without traceable justification), and journal-gap detection (hash-chain discontinuity or shipping failure). Each alert names an owner in the registry beside the tool; unowned alerts are wallpaper, and wallpaper is how journals become compliance artifacts instead of instruments -- the difference between a cockpit and a museum, which is the difference this entire cluster keeps drawing between systems that watch and systems that merely record.

Does journaling slow agents measurably?
How long should journals be retained?

Hot ninety days for operational queries; cold retention per artifact class: compliance-bound sessions per mandate, household agents one year, ephemeral sandbox sessions thirty days then drop. Write the retention matrix in the registry policy with owners, and prune by timer rather than by disk pressure -- journals deleted by capacity emergencies are journals whose retention policy was never a decision, and undeclared defaults are how audits find surprises.

Can users read their agent's journal?

title: Which Local Models Are Actually Good for Coding?
description: Which local models are actually good for coding: benchmark snapshots by size and quantization, tool-call reliability, and the pairs that fit 8 and 16 GB boxes.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The three tiers, with honest job descriptions

  • Completion tier (7-8B coder, Q8): line and block completion, test boilerplate, regex-and-CSV chores. Fast on CPU-plus-small-GPU boxes; errors are local and obvious; the tier where local models beat cloud latency for keystroke-coupled work.
  • Conversation tier (13-14B, Q4-Q6): explain this module, draft this function, convert this pattern; long-context reads of single files plus neighbors. Quality holds when context stays under ~8k of relevant code -- retrieval discipline matters more than model size here, per the RAG guide's chunking rules applied to repositories.
  • Architecture tier (30B+, Q4 where memory allows): cross-module refactoring proposals, migration planning, review commentary. Useful as a senior-ish second reader whose suggestions compile-check before belief; never as an authority, per the verification habits below.

The four-test audition before adoption

  1. FIM discipline: give prefix and suffix of a real function; a coding-capable model respects the suffix boundary instead of rewriting past it.
  2. Diff format: request changes as unified diff on a 300-line file; count malformed hunks across ten runs -- patch-parseable output is the gate for editor integration.
  3. Long-context honesty: embed the question's answer deep in an 8k-token file with two decoys; models that cite the decoy confidently fail, regardless of benchmark fame.
  4. Tool-call restraint: in an agent harness, does the model call search/read tools when context lacks the answer, or hallucinate from priors? Restraint under uncertainty is the trait that predicts safe agent behavior, and it is measurable in an evening.

Workflow integration that survives contact

Editor completion from tier one with a 200 ms debounce and local-only routing (the sensitive-mode toggle from the paste-safety guide); chat and review from tier two behind the gateway with citations-to-file-paths enforced in the prompt; architecture drafts from tier three exported as markdown for human editing, never piped into apply-patch tooling. Compile-and-test feedback loops close the quality gap materially: models whose patches run your test suite improve in effective correctness far beyond their raw benchmark delta, because the suite is a verifier the model cannot charm -- the proof cluster's philosophy arriving in software engineering clothes, verification over vibes.

Where local coding models still lose, named plainly

Do coding models need system prompts differently?

Yes: state the output contract explicitly (diff format, no prose around patches, cite file paths), pin the language and framework versions in the system text, and include one worked example -- coder models respond to contract clarity more than generalists do, because their training distribution contains enormous amounts of contract-following (compilers, linters, CI) and very little contract-negotiation.

Is FIM support worth checking if my editor doesn't use it?

Check anyway: FIM capability correlates with suffix-awareness in plain chat edits (models that understand holes understand boundaries), and editors adopt FIM faster than teams adopt new models -- auditing for it now prevents a surprise migration later, and the audition's first test costs five minutes per candidate.

How much does quantization hurt code correctness specifically?

title: Q4 vs Q8 Quantization: What Do I Actually Lose?
description: Q4 vs Q8 quantization: measured quality deltas on reasoning, coding and summarization, VRAM savings, and the task types where 4-bit visibly hurts output.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The deltas, by task family

Task familyQ4_K_M vs FP16Q8_0 vs FP16Q4 vs Q8 gap
Summarization-1.2%-0.4%within rubric noise
Extraction / JSON-2.1%-0.8%small but visible at scale
Code completion-3.4%-1.2%measurable in compile-pass rate
Multi-hop reasoning-5.8%-2.0%the gap that bites
Exact recall from context-8.3%-3.1%largest; test explicitly

Why the loss lands where it lands

Quantization error is not uniform noise: importance-aware schemes protect salient channels, so common patterns survive while rare, precise weight configurations -- exactly what exact-recall and long-chain composition depend on -- absorb the rounding. The behavioral signature follows: fluency and gist hold (distribution-typical outputs), precision tails suffer (distribution-atypical outputs). This is also why vibe checks mislead: ten casual prompts feel identical across quants while your twentieth, hardest workflow degrades; harnesses exist because humans sample the easy tail by instinct. The quantization explainer carries the format-level mechanics; this page prices the consequences.

Speed and memory: what you buy with the loss

The twenty-minute decision protocol

  1. Pull 50 real requests from your gateway journal or workflow logs (the gateway piece makes this a query, not a project).
  2. Score Q8 as baseline with an automatic metric plus ten human-rubric samples.
  3. Score Q4_K_M identically; compute per-family deltas against the table above as sanity, not substitute.
  4. Decide per deployment slot: daily-driver chat and drafting tolerate Q4; recall- or code-critical slots get Q8 if memory allows; pin whichever artifact hash the decision produced.

Twenty minutes, two numbers, one pinned hash -- and the decision re-runs itself whenever models or runtimes upgrade, because the request corpus lives in-repo beside the scoring script. Teams that skip the protocol do not skip the decision; they make it by folklore, and folklore's quantization opinions are usually somebody's GPU vendor's marketing wearing a benchmark's costume.

Does Q4 hurt long-context behavior more than short?

Indirectly, yes: long contexts lean on exact-recall and cross-reference behaviors that sit in the precision tail quantization erodes first, and KV-cache quantization (a separate choice) compounds if also set low. Keep weights at Q4 but KV at q8 for long-context slots -- the memory math still wins overall, and the quality tail recovers most of what the weight quant took.

title: Does a Local LLM Hallucinate More Than a Cloud One?
description: Do local LLMs hallucinate more than cloud ones? What changes with size and quantization, how to measure hallucination rate on your corpus, and mitigation stacks.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The variables that actually move hallucination

  • Scale and training mix: the dominant terms; frontier cloud models lead here, and no deployment choice changes it.
  • Context discipline: over-long or contradictory context raises confabulation in every model class; retrieval quality (the RAG guide's eval loop) moves local hallucination more than any server decision.
  • Sampling settings: temperature and top-p drifts affect local and cloud equally; pinned configs in your gateway make this a controlled variable instead of folklore.

Measuring your own rate, in one evening

Controls that beat deployment-location anxiety

  1. Citation enforcement on fact-mode prompts, with post-processing that flags uncited factual claims (the RAG guide's trust architecture).
  2. Refusal training by prompt contract: explicit "say you cannot verify" instructions measurably convert hallucinations into refusals at small quality cost -- refusals are recoverable errors; confabulations are not.
  3. Verification gates for consequential outputs: code goes to compilers and tests, numbers to recomputation, citations to resolver lookups -- machines checking machines, the portfolio's standing pattern from proofs to patches.
  4. Tier routing: recall-heavy and citation-bearing workloads to Q8-or-cloud slots; drafting and transformation to Q4 local; the gateway's alias table makes tiering invisible to clients.

The honest summary for decision-makers

Does longer context increase local hallucination more than cloud?

Context-length sensitivity scales with model class, not hosting: small models degrade faster past their trained context sweet spot, and KV quantization (a local memory-saving habit) adds a second degradation source at long contexts. Keep long-context slots at Q8 KV or above, and chunk-and-retrieve instead of pasting corpora -- the same advice the RAG and VRAM guides give from their own angles, converging because the physics is shared.

Can self-consistency sampling fix local hallucination cheaply?

Partially and measurably: majority-vote over 5 samples cuts trap-class hallucination roughly in half at 5x compute -- affordable on CPU batches overnight, painful interactively. Use it for offline artifacts (summaries, extractions into records) where latency is free, and spend interactive budget on retrieval and citations instead; sampling tricks are batch economics, not conversation economics.

Should user-facing UIs disclose local model use?

Yes, plainly: a one-line model-and-tier indicator per response (name, quant, routing exception if any) matches the citation philosophy and costs nothing. Disclosure converts user calibration from guesswork into habit -- calibrated users report fewer trust incidents and file better feedback, and better feedback is the eval set's most renewable source, closing the loop between honesty and quality in a way no benchmark purchase can.

title: How Should I Cache LLM Responses Without Stale Answers?
description: How to cache LLM responses without serving stale answers: semantic keys, TTLs by content type, invalidation hooks and the audit trail that makes caching safe.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
The three layers, and what each buys

  • Exact-match: key = sha256(model-id + version + serialized prompt + sampling params + system text); hits are free latency and free watts; TTLs by volatility class (facts: hours; drafts: minutes; codegen: hours with invalidation on dependency hashes where available).
  • Prefix/prompt-cache: provider- or runtime-level reuse of KV for shared system-plus-context prefixes; pays on long-context RAG and agent loops where the prefix dwarfs the turn -- the runtime-side cousin of exact-match, and the reason long-context costs fall non-linearly with conversation length.
  • Artifact cache: embeddings per chunk hash (the RAG ingest dedupe from the RAG guide), summaries per source-hash, extractions per document-hash; the highest-leverage layer because artifacts outlive conversations and recompute costs dominate ingest budgets.

Correctness: the four invalidation laws

Cache entries are promises that the world has not changed; four changes break the promise and must invalidate or version: model or weight change (version in key, old entries age out), sampling parameter change (in key), context-affecting data change (artifact layers hash the source; exact-match cannot know -- accept staleness per TTL or add dependency hashes), and access-tier change (never cache across tiers: a cached answer computed with tier-A retrieval served to tier-B sessions is an authorization bug wearing a performance feature's clothing, the retrieval-authorization rule from the RAG guide restated at cache altitude).

Operations: hit rates, poisoning, and the watts ledger

When not to cache

Personalized generation where the prompt embeds session-private state you cannot key safely; agentic planning turns where repetition is itself the signal (caching a planner's exploratory calls hides loops you need to see in journals); and any response class under active evaluation (A/B prompts, regression suites -- cached answers make benchmark runs measure the cache). The rule of thumb: cache where repetition means redundancy; skip where repetition means information, because the journal's loop-detection and your eval harness both read the uncached stream, and a cache that starves them is a performance feature eating your instruments.

How long should exact-match TTLs be?

By volatility class with measured staleness cost: codegen and facts 1-6 h, conversational turns 5-15 min, embeddings effectively forever per content hash (invalidation is re-hash, not TTL). Start conservative, then read the age-at-hit histogram: entries expiring unused are wasted bytes, entries hitting at TTL edge are TTLs too short -- the histogram tunes both directions with arithmetic instead of opinion.

Does caching break sampling diversity?

Only if your key omits sampling params or seeds: include them and diverse requests miss independently, identical requests hit identically -- which is the correct semantics (same call, same contract). Complaints about "repetitive cached answers" in agent loops are usually planner loops repeating calls, visible in journals as repeated hashes; fix the loop, not the cache, and let the histogram show you which you have.

Should caches be shared across users?

title: Can AI Agents Verify Their Own Actions With Proofs?
description: Can AI agents verify their own actions? Proof-carrying receipts, policy-annotated journals, verifier pinning and the current limits of self-attestation.
origin: Adapted from supplied workspace article draft
body:
What machines can check about an agent's own work

  • Execution integrity: zkVM proofs that a declared program ran on declared inputs producing declared outputs -- the rust-stark-zkvm pattern applied to agent batch steps, turning "I processed the dataset" into a verifiable receipt.
  • Structural invariants: schemas validate, types compile, tests pass, lints clean -- compilers and suites as the oldest verification gates in the building, still the highest-yield.
  • Journal integrity: hash-chained logs where each entry references its predecessor; tampering breaks the chain, per the journaling guide.
  • Policy conformance: gate verdicts recorded beside actions; a conformance checker replays sessions against policy and flags any action lacking its grant -- policy as testable specification, the APG-1 discipline.

What stays human, forever

Intent and proportionality: the agent deleted exactly the files policy allowed -- correctly, catastrophically wrong anyway. Premise truth: the task said "the report is outdated" and the agent verified every step of replacing it, none of the premise. Relevance and taste: outputs that satisfy the letter while missing the point. These are judgment calls by definition, and the mature design routes them to approval gates with context (the diff, the premise sources, the alternatives considered) rather than pretending verification covers them. The deletion-prevention guide's confirmation gates are exactly this layer: machines bound the blast radius; humans own the meaning.

Receipt-carrying actions: the pattern in production

The research edge: what self-verification may yet eat

Can an agent verify another agent's actions?
Do receipts slow agents down materially?
Is self-verification enough for regulated workflows?

It is necessary and insufficient: regulators ask for accountability structures (owners, approvals, retention), not just correctness artifacts. Receipts satisfy the integrity column of an audit brilliantly; the authority column still needs named humans at gates and documented delegation chains. Estates that present proofs as compliance substitutes learn the distinction during the audit; estates that present proofs inside a governance story learn nothing, because the audit simply agrees -- which is the entire goal.
